text:
Allied Biofuels details export routes for planned $6.1B Uzbekistan SAF project

In New York, The Times of Central Asia reported that Allied Biofuels has disclosed planned export routes that would carry sustainable aviation fuel from its proposed facility in Uzbekistan to customers in Europe and the United Arab Emirates via rail and sea corridors crossing Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Suez Canal.

The routes are set out in a logistics agreement with Latvia-based Pro Logistic Services that was signed during the 5th Tashkent International Investment Forum in June and announced on July 20. It covers the future transport of sustainable aviation fuel and electro-synthetic sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF), rather than immediate exports. The production facility has not yet been built, and Allied Biofuels has said commercial fuel supplies are expected to begin in 2030, according to the report.

Under the agreement, Pro Logistic Services will design and implement a multimodal transport network covering dedicated rail tank cars, port handling, freight forwarding, and marine shipping. The company would coordinate delivery from the project site in Uzbekistan to customers in Europe, the UAE, and other markets, the report added.

Em que estágio está o SAF para aviação?

O SAF, sigla de Sustainable Aviation Fuel, já é produzido comercialmente e utilizado em voos regulares. Seu estágio é industrial, mas a oferta permanece pequena diante do consumo mundial de querosene de aviação.

Companhias aéreas e fabricantes apostam nessa alternativa porque aviões de longo curso dificilmente serão eletrificados com as baterias atuais. O combustível aprovado funciona como componente drop-in, capaz de entrar na rede existente depois de misturado e ajustado às especificações aeronáuticas.

Como óleo usado e resíduos se transformam em combustível?

Não existe uma única fábrica ou reação para produzir SAF. A matéria-prima determina quais etapas serão necessárias para remover oxigênio, impurezas e umidade, reorganizando moléculas até formar hidrocarbonetos adequados às baixas temperaturas e às exigências dos motores.

Quais matérias-primas podem entrar na produção?

A sustentabilidade depende da origem do material e do consumo de energia durante sua conversão. Resíduos normalmente evitam competição direta com alimentos, mas possuem disponibilidade limitada, composição variável e custos próprios de coleta, separação e transporte.

Óleo de cozinha usado coletado em residências e restaurantes.

Gordura animal proveniente de cadeias alimentares.

Palha, bagaço e outros resíduos agrícolas.

Resíduos de madeira e atividades florestais.

Fração orgânica e aproveitável do lixo urbano.

Lodo de tratamento, esterco e resíduos úmidos.

Etanol produzido de açúcares ou materiais celulósicos.

Por que o SAF pode abastecer aviões sem trocar os motores?

O combustível precisa atender requisitos de densidade, estabilidade, congelamento, combustão e segurança. As rotas são avaliadas e certificadas antes do uso, e cada processo recebe um limite de mistura com querosene convencional, frequentemente inferior a cem por cento.

Quando a mistura final atende à especificação aeronáutica, ela pode circular por tanques, aeroportos e motores existentes sem uma adaptação específica. O Departamento de Energia dos Estados Unidos descreve essa compatibilidade, apresentada também no vídeo a seguir.

O SAF costuma custar mais que o querosene fóssil, enquanto óleos usados e gorduras não existem em volume suficiente para atender toda a aviação. Novas rotas exigem refinarias, contratos de longo prazo, energia limpa, certificação e cadeias confiáveis de matérias-primas.

Ele também não elimina o CO₂ liberado durante o voo. A vantagem é calculada pelo ciclo de vida, considerando origem, cultivo, coleta, processamento, transporte e mudanças no uso da terra. text:
For years, NetJets sounded to me like an extravagance in search of a problem. Why would anyone commit hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to fly on private jets when commercial airlines offer lie-flat business class and global route networks at a fraction of the price? Then I began researching how NetJets really works: the economics, the logistics, and the experience on the ground and in the air. Somewhere between spreadsheets and case studies, the appeal started to make sense, not as a status symbol, but as a highly engineered time machine for people whose schedules, businesses, and families demand near-total control over when and how they travel.

The Company Behind the Hype

NetJets is not just another private jet charter brand with slick advertising. It is the original fractional jet ownership company, founded in 1964 and now owned by Berkshire Hathaway, the conglomerate led by Warren Buffett. Over six decades it has grown into the largest private jet operator in the world, with a fleet that industry reports say is roughly the size of the next several competitors combined. In practical terms, that means hundreds of aircraft spread across the United States and Europe, from light jets like the Embraer Phenom 300 to long-range workhorses such as Bombardier Global-series aircraft.

Scale is the unglamorous secret behind NetJets. That size allows the company to guarantee availability, rotate aircraft through heavy maintenance without disrupting customers, and reposition jets more efficiently than smaller operators. A traveler flying from Teterboro to West Palm Beach in February, or from Los Angeles to Aspen at Christmas, may never see the coordination behind the scenes. But it is exactly those peak-day, high-demand trips when having access to the largest private fleet can mean the difference between taking off on schedule and scrambling for alternatives.

The Berkshire Hathaway connection also matters in ways that are not obvious at first glance. Private aviation often involves large up-front payments and long-term contracts. Entrusting several hundred thousand dollars, or even millions, to a small or opaque operator carries real risk if that company stumbles financially. By contrast, many owners take comfort in aligning with a business backed by one of the largest and most conservative holding companies in the world. In an industry where operators sometimes appear and disappear with economic cycles, longevity and balance sheet strength are part of the product.

Understanding NetJets starts with seeing it not as a luxury toy, but as a large, tightly managed transportation network. The jets are the visible tip; underneath is a serious aviation operation employing thousands of pilots, dispatchers, schedulers, and maintenance technicians to keep that network moving every day of the year.

Fractional Ownership: Buying a Slice of a Jet

The model that made NetJets famous is fractional ownership, the idea that you can buy a share of a specific aircraft type rather than owning an entire jet yourself. In a typical arrangement, a 1/16 share equates to about 50 flight hours per year, while larger shares can provide 100, 150, or 200 hours annually. You are not flying in “your” individual airframe every time, but contractually you own a slice of a jet in the fleet and receive guaranteed access to that aircraft type.

On paper, the costs can look eye-watering. Recent industry analyses suggest that, by 2026, first-year costs for a 1/16 share in a popular light jet such as a Phenom 300 can exceed one million dollars once you add the acquisition price, the monthly management fee, and the occupied hourly rate for flight time. For a midsize jet like a Cessna Citation XLS or a super-midsize aircraft such as a Challenger 350, the numbers rise quickly. This is not discretionary money; it is capital that could otherwise sit in a portfolio, fund a new business venture, or buy real estate.

However, fractional ownership is designed for a very particular sort of traveler. Picture a regional private equity partner who spends at least once a week visiting portfolio companies across the Midwest and Sun Belt, often needing to hit two cities and be back home in time for a school event. If that executive is flying 100 to 150 hours per year, wants to reliably depart at 7:15 a.m. from a smaller suburban airport, and cannot afford delays or last-minute cancellations, the math shifts. In that use case, fractional ownership can deliver near-airline-style dispatch reliability, a consistent cabin experience, and the ability to schedule trips with as little as 4 to 10 hours’ notice, even at busy times.

The other subtle advantage is predictability. Instead of shopping for on-demand charter each time and absorbing market swings in hourly rates and aircraft availability, fractional owners lock in many of their costs ahead of time. They know their monthly management fee. They know their occupied hourly rate, subject to fuel and certain surcharges. For the family that charters a jet once or twice a year for ski trips, this kind of certainty is unnecessary. For a law firm whose litigators are shuttling between depositions and hearings in multiple states every month, or a manufacturer whose executives must visit plants in out-of-the-way locations on tight timelines, it becomes a form of operational insurance.

Lease and Jet Card: Access Without Ownership

Not every traveler wants, or needs, the capital commitment of fractional ownership. Recognizing that, NetJets has layered additional access models on top of the original share concept. Leasing mimics fractional ownership in terms of guaranteed availability and access to specific aircraft types, but instead of paying an up-front acquisition price, clients pay a recurring lease fee. Recent public information suggests U.S. leases can begin in the low- to mid-200,000 dollar range per year for entry-level arrangements, plus hourly charges when you actually fly.

Below that sits the NetJets Card, the company’s jet card program. Conceptually, a jet card functions like a preloaded debit card for flight hours. You purchase, for example, 25 hours on a certain class of aircraft, deposit several hundred thousand dollars, and then draw down that balance every time you travel. Independent analyses in 2026 describe a 25-hour NetJets card costing in the broad range of approximately 8,000 to 20,000 dollars per flight hour, depending on cabin size and other factors, placing a typical light- or midsize-jet package well into the six figures. All-in effective hourly costs, once fees and certain adjustments are included, often track close to or above the five-figure mark.

To a leisure traveler, these numbers sound outrageous. To a time-strapped executive comparing them not to economy fares but to the all-in cost of owning a personal aircraft, or to the opportunity cost of burning an entire day on multi-leg commercial flights, they feel different. Jet cards typically carry shorter commitment periods, and NetJets has historically allowed card holders to access a defined category of aircraft with fixed or capped hourly rates over the term of the agreement. For someone who expects to fly under 50 hours per year but wants the convenience of a dedicated private aviation provider, the card can be a trial run before escalating into a lease or share.

Real-world examples illustrate the appeal. Consider a family in Dallas whose children attend school in the Northeast, and who make six to eight roundtrips a year for parents’ weekends, holidays, and emergencies. Commercial options often involve connecting flights through congested hubs, winter weather delays, and limited flexibility around school calendars. A 25-hour card loaded on a midsize jet can cover those key journeys, allowing the family to depart from a smaller airport closer to home, arrive at a convenient general aviation field near campus, and compress what might otherwise be a two-day ordeal into one efficient travel day. They are not flying enough to justify ownership, but too often to keep tolerating the commercial grind.

Service, Reliability, and What You Actually Experience

The marketing glosses over it, but what clients are truly buying from NetJets is not the aircraft; it is a promise. That promise includes operational reliability, consistent service standards, and the ability to call or tap an app and have a flight materialize at a specific time with an experienced crew and a well-maintained jet. While competitors can offer similar aircraft and attractive hourly rates, many cannot match the depth of the network behind each flight.

In practice, that means if a jet goes mechanical before your departure from White Plains to Naples, Florida, there is a high probability that NetJets can substitute another aircraft from its fleet and keep you roughly on schedule. That same redundancy applies on peak travel days such as the Sunday after Thanksgiving or the tail end of the Christmas holidays, when much of the private aviation world is stretched to the limit. Clients report that during the most turbulent years for commercial airlines, having a NetJets share or card meant their critical trips still operated, even as airline schedules melted down.

The onboard experience is intentionally understated. Most cabins are configured in neutral tones with leather club seats, fold-out tables, and a small galley. Depending on aircraft size, you may have a full stand-up cabin, a spacious lavatory, and inflight Wi-Fi fast enough for video calls. Catering can range from simple snacks to full meals brought in from local restaurants and hotels. For a CEO quietly reviewing acquisition documents en route from Chicago to Atlanta, the main luxury is not champagne; it is the ability to work securely and uninterrupted in a door-closed environment.

Another underappreciated element is ground handling. Instead of showing up 90 minutes early at a crowded terminal, waiting in security lines, and boarding en masse, NetJets passengers typically drive directly to a private terminal or fixed-base operator. Check-in can be as simple as confirming identities with a customer service representative and walking straight to the aircraft. For families with young children, elderly parents, or pets, this can dramatically lower the stress of travel. For executives, arriving 15 minutes before departure and boarding immediately turns what would have been unproductive time into usable hours in the office or at home.

The Economics Compared With Other Options

To really understand NetJets, it helps to place it on a spectrum of choices. At one end, there is commercial business or first class, which for many long-haul routes offers a very comfortable experience at a fraction of the cost of private aviation. A New York to London business-class ticket on a major carrier, even at a premium holiday price, may run several thousand dollars. A similar route in a private jet can easily climb into the tens of thousands per hour, making commercial the rational choice for most leisure travel, even for high-net-worth individuals.

Moving up the ladder, on-demand charter allows travelers to book a whole aircraft trip by trip without long-term commitments. Charter works well for occasional flyers who value flexibility and do not need the guarantees that a large fractional provider offers. However, charter pricing is variable. During busy periods, the hourly rate on a light jet from Los Angeles to Jackson Hole for a February ski getaway can be substantially higher than the same route in a shoulder season. Availability can tighten quickly, and mechanical disruptions or crew-time limitations sometimes require last-minute substitutions or delays.

Whole aircraft ownership sits at the opposite end. Buying a jet outright provides unparalleled control but also concentrates all the costs and operational responsibilities on a single owner. Acquisition prices for new business jets range from several million dollars for smaller models to tens of millions for long-range aircraft, not including annual fixed costs such as hangar fees, insurance, crew salaries, maintenance reserves, and inspections. For an individual or family flying 100 to 200 hours a year, owning a jet outright often does not pencil out compared to fractional or card programs, especially once residual value risk is considered.

NetJets threads the needle for travelers whose flying patterns are more consistent than the occasional charter customer, but who either cannot justify or do not desire full ownership. The trade-off is cost versus certainty: you pay premium rates, often above the industry average for basic charter, in exchange for guaranteed access, predictable pricing structures, and an operations team that behaves more like an airline than a boutique broker. For a regional real-estate developer needing to visit four construction sites in three states in a single day, or a medical specialist shuttling between hospitals in cities poorly served by commercial flights, that combination has tangible monetary value.

Sustainability, Safety, and the Intangible Factors

Private aviation is understandably scrutinized for its environmental impact. One of the more surprising aspects of digging into NetJets was how much emphasis the company now places on sustainability, within the limits of current technology. The firm highlights its investments in sustainable aviation fuel, which can significantly reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel when blended and used at scale. It also operates a voluntary offset program that allows owners to fund carbon-reducing projects to balance the emissions from their flights.

Critics correctly point out that no amount of offsets or fuel blending fully erases the environmental footprint of flying privately. A single transcontinental trip on a midsize jet can emit more carbon per passenger than dozens of economy tickets on a modern commercial airliner. For some travelers, this is reason enough to avoid private jets altogether. For others, particularly those whose businesses or philanthropic efforts focus on climate issues, participation in a structured sustainability program is a prerequisite for even considering fractional or card solutions.

Safety is another area where NetJets leans heavily on its scale. The company holds high-level safety certifications and employs its own training programs and simulators for pilots. Larger fleets mean more data on operations, maintenance trends, and human factors, which can feed into more robust safety management systems. For the end user, this shows up in ways that may not be immediately visible, such as standardized cockpit procedures, rigorous duty-time rules for pilots, and proactive maintenance that takes aircraft out of service before issues become problems.

Then there are the intangibles: privacy, discretion, and control over your environment. Celebrities and public figures clearly value slipping in and out of smaller airports with minimal attention. Yet many less famous owners are motivated by more mundane concerns, such as keeping young children out of crowded terminals during flu season, or transporting sensitive prototypes and documents far from the gaze of competitors. NetJets, with its seasoned crews and long-standing relationships with fixed-base operators around the world, effectively sells discretion as part of the fare.

Who NetJets Really Makes Sense For

As I dug deeper into how NetJets works day to day, one conclusion became obvious: this is not a rational product for aspirational flyers who might stretch their finances to sample a taste of private aviation once or twice. The costs are simply too high, and the contracts too involved, for that. Instead, NetJets is engineered for a surprisingly narrow but lucrative audience: individuals and organizations for whom time, predictability, and control are not luxuries but operating requirements.

That might be a family-owned manufacturing business in the Midwest where the leadership team must regularly visit plants in small cities that lack nonstop commercial service. It might be a medical group flying transplant surgeons to regional hospitals on short notice, where life-or-death operations cannot be held hostage by airline delays. It could be a global investor who needs to bounce among second-tier cities in Europe and the United States in a compressed window while maintaining continuous connectivity and privacy to negotiate deals.

In these real-world scenarios, the alternative to NetJets is not a comfortable business-class seat on a widebody over the Atlantic. It is, instead, a patchwork of regional jets, lengthy layovers, unpredictable delays, and the cumulative fatigue of spending countless nights in generic hotels away from home. When a single cancelled commercial flight can derail a multi-day site visit, delay a product launch, or jeopardize a medical procedure, the premium for private aviation buys more than leather seats. It buys resilience.

There is also a psychological component. For some owners, committing to a share, lease, or card effectively forces discipline around travel. Instead of debating each trip and price-shopping itineraries, they know they have a defined bucket of hours to use within a contract term. They can focus on whether a trip is strategically important rather than whether the fare is marginally higher this week than last. For executives and families who already operate at the margins of what time allows, that mental clarity is its own form of luxury.

The Takeaway

Before I researched it, NetJets looked like pure excess, a flying symbol of wealth with little to offer beyond bragging rights. Understanding how it really works revealed something more nuanced. Fractional ownership, leases, and jet cards are not designed to impress; they are engineered to solve a specific, expensive problem: how to move a small number of people exactly where they need to be, exactly when they need to be there, with a very high level of certainty.

That certainty is underpinned by things most marketing campaigns never show: scheduling algorithms, maintenance tracking systems, pilot training pipelines, and the financial ballast of a parent company known for conservative stewardship. The price of entry is undeniably steep, and for the vast majority of travelers, it will never make sense relative to commercial business class or occasional charter. But for those whose livelihoods or family lives depend on compressing three commercial travel days into one, or on reliably reaching locations the airlines barely serve, NetJets’ appeal is less about luxury and more about logistics.

In the end, NetJets operates like a private airline for a very small, very demanding customer base. Its real product is not the gleaming jet parked on the ramp; it is the reclaimed hours, the avoided disruptions, and the quieter, more controlled journeys that happen out of public view. Once you see it through that lens, the company’s enduring popularity among a certain slice of travelers stops being mysterious and starts to look almost inevitable.

FAQ

Q1. Is NetJets cheaper than owning my own private jet?

In most cases, yes, especially if you fly under a few hundred hours per year. Full ownership concentrates all fixed costs on a single user, whereas NetJets spreads acquisition, crew, maintenance, and overhead across many owners. For flyers in the 50 to 200 hours per year range, a NetJets share, lease, or card often provides similar convenience at a lower overall cost than buying and operating an entire aircraft alone.

Q2. How many hours a year do I need to fly before NetJets makes sense?

NetJets tends to make the most sense for travelers who fly regularly but not constantly. If you expect to fly fewer than 25 hours per year, ad hoc charter is usually more economical. Between roughly 25 and 50 hours, a jet card can be attractive. Above that, especially past 50 to 75 hours annually, leasing or fractional ownership can start to deliver better value, provided you care about guaranteed access and predictable pricing.

Q3. What is the difference between a NetJets share, lease, and card?

A share is fractional ownership of an aircraft, with a large up-front acquisition cost, ongoing monthly management fees, and per-hour flight charges. A lease provides similar access and guarantees but substitutes an annual or monthly lease payment for the acquisition cost. A jet card is a prepaid block of flight hours, with a defined hourly rate on a specific cabin class, and typically shorter-term commitments and less capital at risk than ownership or leasing.

Q4. Can I choose the exact aircraft I fly on with NetJets?

In most programs you select an aircraft type or cabin category, not a specific tail number. For example, you might contract for access to a midsize jet model. NetJets then assigns you a particular aircraft in that category based on availability and operational needs. You enjoy a consistent cabin size and performance profile, but you are not tied to one physical jet for every trip.

Q5. How much notice do I need to give to book a NetJets flight?

The required notice depends on your specific contract and time of year, but one of the selling points of NetJets is relatively short lead times. Fractional owners in many programs can book with around a day or two of notice, and in some cases as little as several hours, even during busy periods. Jet card holders generally have slightly longer notice requirements, particularly on peak travel days.

Q6. Are NetJets flights safer than standard charter flights?

Safety records are influenced by many factors, but NetJets emphasizes standardized training, dedicated maintenance, and a structured safety management system that benefits from operating a large, homogeneous fleet. Many charter operators also maintain excellent safety standards, yet NetJets’ scale allows for more centralized control over pilot training, scheduling, and aircraft upkeep, which appeals to risk-conscious travelers.

Q7. How does NetJets handle delays or mechanical issues?

If your assigned aircraft develops a mechanical issue before departure, NetJets often has the ability to substitute another jet from its fleet, minimizing delays. The company also manages crew duty limits, weather decisions, and rerouting in a coordinated way, similar to an airline operations center. While delays can still occur, the breadth of the fleet and centralized control give NetJets more tools to recover a disrupted trip than smaller providers typically have.

Q8. What are the environmental impacts of flying with NetJets?

Flying privately always carries a higher per-passenger carbon footprint than traveling in commercial economy. NetJets has introduced measures such as access to sustainable aviation fuel and optional carbon offset programs to mitigate some of that impact, but these do not completely neutralize emissions. Environmentally conscious travelers need to weigh the benefits of flexibility and time savings against the higher climate cost of private aviation.

Q9. Can businesses deduct the cost of NetJets programs?

Whether NetJets expenses are deductible depends on how the flights are used, applicable tax rules, and the structure of the business. Many companies treat NetJets costs as legitimate business travel expenses when flights directly support operations, client work, or revenue-generating activities. Because tax treatment is complex and can change, prospective users should consult qualified tax and legal advisors before committing to a share, lease, or card.

text:
China has unveiled a daring new plan to integrate artificial intelligence throughout the nuclear energy life cycle. This week, at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) revealed a new plan for safely integrating artificial intelligence into the nuclear sector, called ADANES – the Accelerator-Driven Advanced Nuclear Energy System. The system “fundamentally changes the safety logic that governs conventional nuclear reactors” and marks a major turning point in the AI revolution as well as the global nuclear renaissance.

While nuclear disasters are historically rare, their potential fallout is massive. But there is potential for artificial intelligence to lessen this risk. According to Interesting Engineering, “Disasters like Chernobyl and Fukushima have reminded us time and again, that the risk of an accident remains with this technology, and we need to prepare for the worst scenarios. A technology like AI is well suited for this role as it can process large number of signals coming in from an operational reactor and shut it down in the earliest stages of a mishap.”

Wang Shoujun, the president of the Chinese Nuclear Society, makes the argument that the integration of large language models into every corner of the economy, including nuclear energy, is an inevitability. By accepting this as fact, the scientists behind the ADANES believe that the responsible thing to do is get ahead of the trend and focus on planning and safety measures, rather than trying to prevent AI from infiltrating the nuclear power sector. Wang says that, through the use of ADANES, “AI will play a core role throughout the full life cycle of nuclear energy by improving quality, efficiency and safety.”

However, today's large language models operate under great opacity, and this ‘black box’ functionality is fundamentally at odds with stringent nuclear energy safety requirements. We need a far greater level of transparency and a deeper understanding of how large language models work and will be applied in this context. According to a recent report from China Daily, ADANES can be used to establish such an understanding.

“The AI architecture consists of five layers — a unified data infrastructure, physics-native world models, physical-system control, intelligent-agent coordination and continuous evolution — embedding AI throughout the system's full life cycle, from design and commissioning to operation and maintenance,” the report states. China is also developing a national-scale supportive infrastructure to provide an “engineering verification platform” for ADANES in order to shore up the long-term stability and viability of the system.

It’s true that the artificial intelligence boom is already finding its way into the nuclear energy sector in various ways and to varying degrees. Earlier this year, tech giants Microsoft and NVIDIA announced that they are jointly rolling out an AI-powered toolkit designed to cut down on arduous permitting, design, and engineering processes that have made new nuclear plants notoriously slow and expensive to build in the United States.

Ushering in a new digital era for nuclear power, the toolkit “provides end-to-end tools that combine AI and digital twins for creating faster iterative design and engineering solutions,” according to a March report from Interesting Engineering. “Licensing and permitting is handled by Generative AI for document drafting and gap analysis.”

Furthermore, the push to develop new and advanced nuclear energy generation capacity is also being largely driven by the AI boom. Silicon Valley is getting increasingly involved in funding and developing next-gen nuclear technologies in order to fuel the rapidly growing energy demands of generative AI, which are projected to far outstrip energy additions unless we make some major breakthroughs. China is not the only nation making unsettlingly daring decisions when it comes to nuclear power. A wave of U.S.-based startups is also eagerly crowding into the sector with concerning disregard for safety measures, creating a concerning security environment in the world's largest economies.

Saturday July 25, 2026

Governor Walz Celebrates Opening of Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuel Hub

On Friday, Governor Walz joined elected officials and leaders from Delta Airlines, Ecolab, and Flint Hills Resources to celebrate the completion of the Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) Hub.

“We’re seeing the devastating effects of climate change in our forests right now. That’s why Minnesota is building the sustainable innovations of the future,” said Governor Walz. “Our new sustainable aviation fuel hub is reducing our carbon footprint, supporting our farmers, and creating jobs.”

Located at Flint Hills Resources’ Pine Bend Refinery in Rosemount, the facility can accommodate up to 30 million gallons of neat SAF annually, blend it with conventional jet fuel and deliver blended SAF to MSP Airport through existing pipeline infrastructure. With this capability in place, SAF can now be supplied, blended, and uplifted at MSP Airport in commercial volumes, enabling use of Minnesota’s nation-leading SAF tax credit and solving a critical infrastructure bottleneck.

Governor Walz Celebrates Three Consecutive Months of Job Growth

Governor Walz celebrated three consecutive months of job growth following losses seen during Operation Metro Surge. The Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED) announced that Minnesota added 13,200 jobs in June, outpacing the national rate.

“Minnesota continues to be a leader in economic recovery and expansion despite national uncertainty,” said Governor Walz. “Continued job growth reflects our strategic investments in workforce training, the prioritization of job protections, and support of small businesses impacted by federal operations.”

Last week, Governor Walz announced Minnesota’s rank as a top state in the nation for business. Minnesota ranks fifth overall, placing top ten in quality of life, infrastructure, and economic environment.

Since 2019, Governor Walz has helped create 95,000 new jobs, a 3.2% increase. During this time the number of business establishments in the state grew by more than 35,600 and average weekly wages grew $334, an increase of almost 30%.

ICYMI: Governor Walz, Executive Council Receive Wildfire Briefing, Extend Peacetime Emergency

Last week, Governor Walz convened a meeting of the Executive Council to receive a briefing on the spread of wildfires across northeastern Minnesota. The council voted to extend the peacetime emergency declared in Executive Order 26-08, authorizing continued state assistance and support for 30 days.

“Wildfires spreading across northern Minnesota are posing an increasing threat to lives, property, and our wilderness,” said Governor Walz. “We are staging a coordinated response with state and local partners and extending resources to manage the fires. I am incredibly grateful for the partnership of our Canadian allies and for the tireless work of our firefighters, first responders, and Minnesota National Guard members on the front line, keeping Minnesotans safe.”

Amidst unusually dry, hot, and windy weather, wildfires have quickly spread across northern Minnesota, including throughout the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW). The fast moving and rapidly shifting fires pose threats to lives, property, and critical infrastructure, and prompted closure of public access to the BWCAW.

text:
Kecelakaan maut yang merenggut nyawa seorang pelajar di Jalan Mayor Zen, Palembang, mendorong Pemerintah Provinsi Sumatera Selatan mengevaluasi tata kelola lalu lintas di kawasan tersebut. Gubernur Sumsel Herman Deru menegaskan penanganan tidak cukup hanya memperbaiki jalan berlubang, tetapi juga harus mengkaji ulang Analisis Dampak Lalu Lintas (Amdal Lalin) di koridor itu.

Desakan evaluasi muncul setelah AF (14), siswi SMAN 5 Palembang, meninggal dunia usai sepeda motor yang ditumpanginya diduga kehilangan kendali saat menghindari lubang di jalan. Korban terjatuh dan terlindas truk Fuso yang melaju searah dari belakang.

Menurut Herman Deru, penyebab utama kecelakaan harus dipastikan lebih dahulu agar langkah penanganan yang dilakukan benar-benar tepat sasaran.

“Dicek dulu apakah memang karena jalan berlubang atau ada faktor lain. Kalau memang karena jalannya berlubang, kita minta segera diperbaiki,” ujarnya, Jumat (24/7/2026).

Namun, ia menegaskan evaluasi tidak boleh berhenti pada aspek infrastruktur semata. Jika penyebab kecelakaan berkaitan dengan pola lalu lintas, maka analisis dampak lalu lintas di kawasan tersebut harus diperbaiki.

“Kalau bukan karena kondisi jalan, tentu kita ingin memperbaiki analisis dampak lalu lintasnya. Apa yang sebenarnya sering terjadi di lokasi itu,” tegasnya.

text:
European airlines are accelerating their investment in digital aviation technologies as they seek to improve operational efficiency, strengthen sustainability initiatives and support more consistent flight performance. The latest development comes as ITA Airways and Austrian Airlines have expanded their use of software solutions from GE Aerospace that transform operational flight data into practical insights for airline teams and pilots.

The agreements reflect a broader shift within the aviation industry towards data-driven decision-making. Rather than relying solely on new aircraft or infrastructure investments to improve efficiency, airlines are increasingly adopting digital tools that help optimise everyday flight operations. The objective is to reduce unnecessary fuel consumption, improve operational consistency and support long-term environmental goals while maintaining high standards of safety.

European Airlines Continue Their Digital Transformation

Airline operations have become increasingly data-intensive, with aircraft generating large volumes of operational information during every flight. Modern software platforms allow airlines to analyse this information and identify opportunities to improve flight planning, fuel use and operational performance.

GE Aerospace has announced that ITA Airways will implement Fuel Insight and FlightPulse, two software applications designed to help airlines convert operational data into actionable information.

Fuel Insight enables airline departments responsible for flight operations, dispatch and fuel management to monitor fuel performance and identify areas where greater efficiency may be achieved. FlightPulse extends these capabilities by providing pilots with flight-specific operational insights before and after each journey, allowing informed decisions based on actual flight data.

Together, these solutions support closer coordination between airline operational teams and flight crews, helping improve efficiency across daily operations.

ITA Airways Focuses on Fuel Efficiency

Fuel remains one of the largest operating costs for commercial airlines and continues to be a major area of focus across the aviation industry.

By introducing Fuel Insight and FlightPulse, ITA Airways aims to strengthen its ability to monitor fuel performance, evaluate operational trends and support consistent implementation of fuel-saving procedures.

According to GE Aerospace, the software is designed to help airlines understand operational performance across different flights while enabling departments to measure progress using shared operational information.

The system also integrates with GE Aerospace’s Event Measurement System (EMS), creating a connected workflow between operational analytics and airline decision-making.

Rather than replacing existing procedures, the platform provides additional information that helps operational teams identify opportunities to improve efficiency throughout normal airline operations.

Austrian Airlines Expands Digital Flight Operations

Austrian Airlines, a member of the Lufthansa Group, has also expanded its cooperation with GE Aerospace by adopting FlightPulse.

The airline already uses GE Aerospace’s Safety Insight, Fuel Insight and the EMS platform for flight data analysis. The addition of FlightPulse extends these capabilities by making operational information directly available to pilots through a mobile application.

This approach allows flight crews to review relevant operational insights before departure and after landing, supporting decisions associated with safety, fuel awareness and operational consistency.

Providing pilots with direct access to operational information forms part of the airline’s wider digital transformation strategy, enabling data to support decision-making at every stage of flight operations.

Flight Data Supports Better Operational Decisions

Commercial aircraft generate valuable operational information throughout every flight. Analysing this information enables airlines to identify patterns that may improve efficiency across fleets.

Flight analytics platforms examine operational trends including fuel usage, aircraft performance and flight procedures. Airlines can then use these insights to review operational practices, support pilot training and monitor improvements over time.

By making operational information more accessible, airlines can encourage greater consistency in the application of fuel-saving procedures while supporting continuous operational improvement.

This data-driven approach is becoming an increasingly important component of modern airline management as carriers seek to improve performance without compromising safety or operational standards.

Digital Technology Supports Aviation Sustainability

The aviation industry continues to explore multiple pathways to reduce its environmental impact.

Alongside investments in more efficient aircraft, sustainable aviation fuel and operational improvements, digital technologies are playing a growing role in reducing unnecessary fuel consumption.

According to GE Aerospace, deployments of Fuel Insight and FlightPulse across airlines using its Software as a Service platform have been associated with approximately fifteen percent higher adoption of fuel-saving procedures and around twenty percent higher success rates for sustainability procedures.

The company also reports that, during the first year of programme use, participating deployments have averaged approximately five point seven one million kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions avoided and around one point eight eight million kilograms of fuel saved.

These figures illustrate how operational improvements supported by digital analytics can complement broader aviation sustainability strategies.

Smarter Flight Operations Benefit Airlines and Travellers

Although the technology primarily supports airline operations, improvements in operational efficiency can also contribute to a more consistent passenger experience.

Better operational planning enables airlines to monitor flight performance more effectively while encouraging consistent operational procedures across fleets.

Digital flight analytics also improve communication between operational departments, dispatch teams and pilots, allowing decisions to be based on shared information rather than isolated data sources.

As more airlines adopt advanced operational analytics, passengers may increasingly benefit from more predictable operations supported by better-informed decision-making behind the scenes.

Software Is Becoming Central to Modern Aviation

The aviation industry has entered a period in which software is becoming as important as physical infrastructure.

Aircraft continue to become more technologically advanced, but the ability to analyse operational information is now emerging as a critical competitive advantage for airlines.

Digital platforms enable carriers to identify trends more quickly, monitor operational performance more accurately and support continuous improvements without requiring major structural changes to existing operations.

For European airlines such as ITA Airways and Austrian Airlines, investment in operational analytics reflects a long-term commitment to efficiency, sustainability and innovation.

Outlook for Digital Airline Operations

The agreements announced by GE Aerospace demonstrate how airlines are increasingly integrating digital technology into everyday operations.

By expanding access to operational flight data and supporting more informed decision-making among both operational teams and pilots, ITA Airways and Austrian Airlines are strengthening their digital capabilities while supporting fuel efficiency and sustainability objectives.

As airlines continue balancing operational costs, environmental responsibilities and growing passenger demand, software-driven operational intelligence is expected to play an increasingly significant role across commercial aviation.

Rather than replacing traditional operational expertise, advanced analytics provide airline teams with additional information that supports safer, more efficient and more sustainable flight operations, helping shape the next phase of digital aviation across Europe.

text:
세계에서 가장 많은 국가로 운항하는 터키항공(Turkish Airlines)이 친환경 항공기 연료인 지속가능항공유(SAF) 생산 기반을 다지기 위한 글로벌 펀드에 본격 합류했다. 터키항공은 지속가능항공유(Sustainable Aviation Fuel, 이하 SAF)의 활성화를 도모하는 'SAFFA Fund(Sustainable Aviation Fuel Financing Alliance Fund)'에 자금을 출적하며 탄소 저감 행보에 속도를 낸다. 이번 결정은 차세대 항공 생태계를 구축함과 동시에 장기적으로 지속가능항공유(SAF)의 안정적인 수급을 도모하고, 항공 여정에서 발생하는 온실가스를 감축하겠다는 취지다.

승객의 친환경 여정을 돕는 지속가능항공유 공급망 확충

2023년 12월 첫발을 뗀 SAFFA Fund는 지속가능항공유(SAF)의 생산 인프라를 증설하고 항공 분야의 탈탄소화를 촉진하기 위해 조성된 전문 투자펀드다. 기술적 성숙도가 확보된 지속가능항공유(SAF) 프로젝트를 주요 대상으로 삼고 있으며, 다양한 생산 기술과 지역을 망라한 투자 포트폴리오를 통해 전 세계적인 연료 공급망 확립에 기여하고 있다.

이번 펀드 참여를 계기로 터키항공은 미래 항공 산업을 선도할 지속가능항공유 생산 사업 및 원료 연구, 혁신 기술 개발 부문의 협력을 확대하고 장기적인 연료 수급 안정성을 확보할 방침이다. 이에 더해 에어버스(Airbus)와의 지속가능성 협력을 한층 공고히 하면서, 환경친화적인 항공업계 전환과 글로벌 공급망의 안정성을 도모하기 위한 공동 노력을 이어갈 예정이다.

항공사와 승객이 함께 만드는 친환경 가치 소비

레벤트 코눅추(Levent Konukcu) 터키항공 투자전략총괄(CISO)은 "SAFFA Fund 참여는 지속가능항공유(SAF) 생태계의 성장을 뒷받침하는 동시에 미래 항공산업의 혁신을 끌어갈 프로젝트에 투입되는 전략적 결정"이라며, "글로벌 파트너들과의 연대를 통해 지속가능항공유의 공급 안정성을 높이고 국제 항공산업의 친환경 전환을 앞당기는 데 기여하겠다"라고 밝혔다.

마이클 디키 모건(Michael Dickey Morgan) 번햄 스털링 에셋 매니지먼트(Burnham Sterling Asset Management) 전무이사는 "SAFFA Fund는 다양한 기술과 지역에 걸친 지속가능항공유 사업에 자본을 투입하도록 설계된 투자 플랫폼"이라며, "터키항공의 동참은 펀드 운용 전략을 한층 강화하는 한편, 지속가능항공유 투자에 대한 산업계의 신뢰와 지속 가능한 비행을 향한 의지를 보여주는 의미 있는 본보기"라고 설명했다.

터키항공에 대한 국내 홍보를 담당하는 에이뷰코리아의 권안나 매니저는 "최근 한국 여행객을 포함한 전 세계 소비자들이 항공사를 선택할 때 기업의 지속가능성과 환경 보호 노력을 중요하게 평가하고 있다"라며 "이번 지속가능항공유 투자 확대를 통해 국내 독자와 여행자들에게도 환경적 책임을 다하는 친환경 비행 경험과 높은 가치를 선사할 수 있을 것으로 기대한다"라고 전했다.

여행자의 발걸음마다 더해지는 환경 보호의 가치

최근 항공을 이용하는 여행자들 사이에서는 단순한 이동을 넘어 환경에 미치는 영향을 최소화하려는 '가치 소비' 트렌드가 확산하고 있다. 항공기 운항 과정에서 지속가능항공유를 혼합 사용하는 비율이 늘어날수록, 승객들이 기내에 탑승하여 이동하는 동안 발생하는 개별 탄소발자국 역시 실질적으로 감소하게 된다. 친환경 연료 공급망이 안정적으로 안착하면, 승객들은 환경 부담을 덜고 더욱 가벼운 마음으로 전 세계 다양한 목적지로의 여정을 즐길 수 있게 된다.

1933년 5대의 항공기로 시작해 글로벌 항공동맹인 스타 얼라이언스(Star Alliance)의 주요 회원사로 성장한 터키항공(Turkish Airlines)은 현재 556대의 항공기를 운용하며 튀르키예(Türkiye) 이스탄불(Yeşilköy-Istanbul)을 거점으로 전 세계 133개국 358개 목적지를 이어주고 있다. 하늘길을 이용하는 전 세계 독자들과 여행자들의 환경 의식이 높아지는 만큼, 항공사의 이 같은 지속가능항공유 투자 노력은 향후 여행객들이 항공사를 선택하는 중요한 기준이자 항공 여정 전체의 가치를 높이는 핵심 동력이 될 것으로 기대된다.

text:
NEW ULM — Hundreds of people of all ages got a slice of working farm life at the Steve and Kerry Hoffman farm Thursday.

Sponsored by the Farm-City Hub Club, Family Night on a Farm was nothing new to the Hoffmans. They have hosted the event many times since it began in 2007.

The free event includes farm tours, hayrides, milking demonstrations, animal petting and other kid’s activities, photos with dairy princesses, educational exhibits and displays, picnic meal, goodie bags, dairy treats including 1919 Root Beer floats, and a chance to meet a veterinarian and other agriculture specialists.

“I think this is our ninth time hosting Family Night on a Farm,” said Steve Hoffman. “We host this event to give urban/city people a chance to get out on a farm.”

He began milking 40 cows in a stanchion barn in 1986. A compost barn and herd expansion took place in 2004. The farm’s original barn was remodeled and a new milking parlor was built in 2005.

The Hoffman’s son Joe joined their farm operation in 2019.

Two years ago, he left the dairy business and began raising beef animals including mostly Angus cows instead of Holsteins for milking.

“I still remember when the last truck with our Holsteins pulled out of driveway,” said Hoffman. “The farm place seemed strange for a while without the mooing.”

They still live on their farm and don’t plan to leave any time soon. Last year, he became an independent insurance agent and his wife Kerry began a dog boarding business.

Steve Hoffman compared Holstein and Angus cows.

“Feeding beef breed cows is way different than it is for dairy cows,” he said. “Beef cows don’t require nearly as many nutritional goodies that dairy cows do. title: A new high-density Airbus A220 enters service in 2027: the redesign that squeezes in more seats
description:
It can lower emissions per passenger, but not automatically if lower costs trigger more flights or if the extra seats fly empty.
Airbus says the A220 can deliver up to a 14 percent lower operating cost per seat, depending on the comparison and configuration.
Lars Wagner, chief executive of Airbus Commercial Aircraft, said the A220 combines “low operating costs” with the range needed to open new markets.
Airbus is still working to increase A220 production and improve the economics of a program that has struggled to reach profitability.
It can lower cost and emissions per occupied seat while giving Airbus more time to strengthen production, but it does not guarantee lower total emissions.
text:
Airbus is preparing the most important practical update yet for its smallest commercial jet. The A220 is gaining a new Airspace cabin with larger, lighter overhead bins, while industry reporting says the A220-300 is being readied for a high-density 160-seat configuration targeted for certification in 2027.

The headline is ten extra seats. So is the denser A220 actually greener? It can lower emissions per passenger, but not automatically if lower costs trigger more flights or if the extra seats fly empty.

More seats without a new jet

AirAsia is now the launch customer for the 160-seat layout after placing a firm order for 150 A220-300s. Airbus says the extra capacity comes from ten additional seats and an extra overwing exit on each side, rather than a stretched fuselage or a new aircraft type. By the end of May 2026, the A220 had recorded 1,109 historical orders and 517 deliveries.

The timing needs a little care. Industry reporting says Airbus has aimed for certification in 2027, while the company’s June 2026 fact sheet still lists the 160-seat version as “certification to come.” AirAsia’s first deliveries are expected in 2028, so 2027 is better understood as a certification target than a guaranteed first passenger flight.

The environmental case

Airbus says the A220 uses 25 percent less fuel and produces 25 percent less carbon dioxide per seat than previous-generation small single-aisle jets. It also reports about 40 percent fewer nitrogen oxide emissions than the CAEP/8 regulatory benchmark, while the A220-300 can fly about 3,913 miles.

There is a simple reason airlines like the denser cabin. If a flight used exactly the same amount of fuel, dividing that trip across 160 seats instead of 150 would reduce fuel per available seat by about 6 percent. Real flights will carry more passenger and baggage weight, so the actual gain will be smaller, but the direction is clear.

Still, efficiency per seat is not the same as lower total emissions. ICCT research warns that traffic growth can overwhelm gains from more efficient aircraft and sustainable aviation fuel. A greener plane can help, but it is not a free pass for unlimited growth.

A cabin passengers will notice

The Airspace update is more visible than the engineering work behind the new seating limit. Airbus says the overhead bins offer 20 percent more volume, hold up to 15 percent more bags on the A220-300, and are 10 percent lighter. The redesigned cabin structure is about 300 pounds lighter overall.

That sounds minor until boarding starts and the last carry-on has nowhere to go. More bin space can reduce gate checking and speed up the scramble to find room, while lighter components save a small amount of fuel on every trip. Air Canada is the launch customer for the upgraded cabin.

The lighting also changes the mood. The system offers more than 16 million LED colors that airlines can match to their branding or different phases of flight, and Airbus plans to make the cabin available as a retrofit in the coming years.

Why airlines want it

For carriers, the attraction is straightforward. Ten more seats can spread crew, airport, maintenance, and ownership costs across a larger number of tickets, especially at airports where takeoff and landing slots are scarce. Airbus says the A220 can deliver up to a 14 percent lower operating cost per seat, depending on the comparison and configuration.

AirAsia also sees the smaller jet as a way to open thinner routes and free larger aircraft for longer services. Lars Wagner, chief executive of Airbus Commercial Aircraft, said the A220 combines “low operating costs” with the range needed to open new markets. In practical terms, that means an airline can test a route without sending a bigger A320 family jet half full.

There is another business layer. Airbus is still working to increase A220 production and improve the economics of a program that has struggled to reach profitability. A higher-capacity cabin is a relatively low-risk way to make the existing jet more valuable before the company commits to a longer and costlier derivative.

What passengers may give up

The A220’s basic five-across cabin does not change, and Airbus still promotes economy seats wider than 18 inches. Airbus has not detailed a single standard 160-seat floor plan, which means the final balance of seat pitch and service space will be airline-specific.

That is where the trade-off becomes personal. Passengers may get better bins and modern lighting, yet a high-density layout can leave less cabin floor per traveler. The plane may feel brighter and smarter while also feeling busier.

The A220-500 question

For years, airlines and lessors have asked whether Airbus will stretch the aircraft into an A220-500 with capacity closer to the A320. No launch decision has been announced, although Quebec said in July 2026 that discussions are underway and that it could support the project with Canada if Airbus proceeds.

For now, the 160-seat A220-300 is the bridge. It can lower cost and emissions per occupied seat while giving Airbus more time to strengthen production, but it does not guarantee lower total emissions.

text:
Jakarta: Di tengah dinamika lanskap energi global yang semakin kompleks, PT Pertamina Hulu Energi (PHE) terus memperkuat langkah strategisnya dalam menjaga keberlanjutan pasokan energi nasional. Melalui pengembangan portofolio eksplorasi yang dilakukan secara konsisten dalam lima tahun terakhir, PHE berhasil memperluas wilayah operasi melalui akuisisi Wilayah Kerja (WK) baru serta pelaksanaan Joint Study (JS) bersama sejumlah mitra strategis, baik di dalam maupun luar negeri.

Upaya ini merupakan bagian dari komitmen PHE untuk menjawab tantangan meningkatnya kebutuhan energi nasional sekaligus mengantisipasi penurunan produksi alamiah (natural decline) pada wilayah kerja eksisting. Dengan memperluas area eksplorasi dan membuka peluang penemuan sumber daya baru, PHE terus memperkuat fondasi ketahanan energi Indonesia untuk jangka panjang.

Pertamina Hulu Energi perluas portofolio eksplorasi melalui kolaborasi global dan akuisisi wilayah kerja baru. (Dok. Istimewa)

Sebagai tahapan awal yang sangat menentukan dalam mengidentifikasi potensi sumber daya migas sekaligus membuka peluang pengembangan wilayah kerja baru, PHE secara aktif menjalin kolaborasi melalui kegiatan Joint Study bersama berbagai perusahaan energi kelas dunia. Kolaborasi ini tidak hanya menjadi wadah berbagi keahlian dan teknologi, tetapi juga memperkuat sinergi dalam mengeksplorasi potensi cekungan migas yang masih belum berkembang di Indonesia.

Berdasarkan data Direktorat Jenderal Minyak dan Gas Bumi (Ditjen Migas) hingga April 2026, PHE menjadi perusahaan dengan jumlah Joint Study terbanyak di Indonesia, yakni sebanyak 10 studi. Hingga Juli 2026, jumlah tersebut meningkat menjadi 12 Joint Study, terdiri atas 10 studi yang masih berjalan, satu studi telah selesai, dan satu studi lainnya tengah menunggu persetujuan pemerintah.

Joint Study tersebut dilaksanakan bersama sejumlah perusahaan energi internasional bereputasi tinggi, seperti Petronas, BP, ENI, KUFPEC, SK Earthon, PetroChina, POSCO, TPAO, Woodside, serta mitra strategis lainnya. Area studi mencakup berbagai wilayah prospektif dari Indonesia bagian barat hingga timur. Di tingkat regional, PHE juga memperluas kerja sama dengan Management Petroleum Malaysia (MPM) melalui skema Technical Evaluation Agreement (TEA) pada beberapa blok migas di Malaysia.

Seluruh kolaborasi tersebut menjadi sarana pertukaran pengetahuan, teknologi, dan kapabilitas teknis dalam mengidentifikasi play type baru yang berpotensi menjadi sumber cadangan migas masa depan. Kepercayaan yang diberikan para mitra global juga mencerminkan pengakuan terhadap kompetensi PHE sebagai National Oil Company (NOC) yang mampu bersaing di tingkat internasional.

Selain memperkuat kolaborasi melalui Joint Study, PHE juga terus memperluas portofolio eksplorasinya. Sepanjang periode 2023–2026, PHE berhasil memperoleh delapan wilayah kerja eksplorasi baru di Indonesia, yaitu Bunga, Peri Mahakam, East Natuna, Melati, Binaiya, Lavender, Bobara, dan North Ketapang, serta satu wilayah kerja eksplorasi di Malaysia, yakni Blok SK-510.

Pada seluruh wilayah kerja tersebut, PHE berkomitmen menjalankan berbagai program eksplorasi sesuai komitmen kerja pasti, mulai dari studi geologi dan geofisika (G&G), akuisisi data seismik, hingga pemboran eksplorasi. Langkah ini diharapkan mampu mengoptimalkan potensi hidrokarbon sekaligus mempercepat penemuan cadangan baru sebagai penopang produksi migas nasional di masa mendatang.

Direktur Eksplorasi PT Pertamina Hulu Energi, Asep Samsul Arifin, mengatakan bahwa strategi ekspansi yang dijalankan PHE merupakan bagian dari upaya membangun portofolio eksplorasi yang sehat dan berkelanjutan.

"Eksplorasi merupakan investasi jangka panjang bagi keberlanjutan industri hulu migas. Melalui perluasan wilayah kerja, penguatan kolaborasi dengan mitra global, serta penerapan teknologi eksplorasi yang semakin maju, kami terus membangun portofolio yang berkualitas untuk meningkatkan peluang penemuan sumber daya migas baru. Langkah ini menjadi bagian dari komitmen PHE dalam mendukung ketahanan dan kemandirian energi nasional," ujar Asep.

Kinerja agresif PHE dalam memperluas area eksplorasi juga memperoleh pengakuan di tingkat global. Berdasarkan data S&P Global tahun 2026 untuk periode 2021–2025, PHE tercatat sebagai National Oil Company (NOC) dengan penambahan luas area eksplorasi baru terbesar di dunia, mencapai lebih dari 90.000 kilometer persegi. Capaian tersebut melampaui sejumlah perusahaan migas nasional dunia, seperti Petronas, PTTEP, ADNOC, maupun Sinopec.

Berbagai pencapaian tersebut menjadi kontribusi nyata PHE dalam mendukung agenda Asta Cita Presiden Prabowo Subianto, khususnya percepatan swasembada energi melalui penguatan kegiatan eksplorasi secara masif, peningkatan penemuan cadangan migas baru, serta penguatan kapasitas produksi nasional.

Ke depan, PHE akan terus memperluas portofolio wilayah kerja eksplorasi maupun produksi, baik di Indonesia maupun di luar negeri. Perusahaan juga berkomitmen mempercepat komersialisasi seluruh potensi eksplorasi, baik pada aset eksisting maupun blok-blok baru hasil ekspansi bisnis. Dengan mengedepankan keunggulan operasional, inovasi teknologi, dan prinsip keberlanjutan, PHE optimistis dapat terus berperan sebagai penggerak utama dalam mewujudkan kedaulatan energi Indonesia.

PHE akan terus berinvestasi dalam pengelolaan operasi dan bisnis hulu migas sesuai prinsip Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG). PHE juga senantiasa berkomitmen Zero Tolerance on Bribery dengan memastikan pencegahan atas fraud dan memastikan perusahaan bersih dari penyuapan. Salah satunya dengan implementasi Sistem Manajemen Anti Penyuapan (SMAP) yang telah terstandardisasi ISO 37001:2016.

text:
The UK is expanding its support for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) projects, broadening financing criteria and releasing updated provisional data for its SAF mandate.1 These measures aim to accelerate the development and adoption of low-carbon aviation alternatives, aligning with the nation's decarbonisation targets. This proactive stance underscores a commitment to fostering a future where clean energy solutions are abundant across all sectors, including aviation.

The UK's strategic push for Sustainable aviation fuel

SAF is a critical component for decarbonising the aviation sector, a key part of the UK's broader energy transition. The government's initiatives reflect a refusal to settle for energy scarcity, instead challenging the notion that aviation must remain a high-carbon industry.

Why SAF is crucial for aviation decarbonisation

Aviation is one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonise due to the high energy density required for flight and the long development cycles for new aircraft technologies. SAF offers a viable solution as it can significantly reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions compared to conventional jet fuel. The UK government has set a legally binding target to reach net-Zero emissions by 2050, with aviation playing its part through the Jet Zero Strategy.

Overview of the UK's SAF mandate and goals

The UK's SAF Mandate came into effect on 1 January 2025, placing a legal obligation on fuel suppliers to blend SAF into jet fuel. The mandate requires SAF to account for at least 2% of all jet fuel in flights taking off from the UK in 2025, increasing to 10% by 2030 and 22% by 2040. The Department for Transport released updated provisional data on 23 July 2026. The SAF mandate is a key part of the UK's alternative aviation fuel policy.

Expanding financing and investment in UK SAF

Scaling SAF production requires significant investment, technological advancement, and robust supply chain development. The UK government is actively implementing policy and financial mechanisms to accelerate SAF development and adoption.

New criteria for SAF project funding

UK Export Finance (UKEF), the country's export credit agency, announced on 23 July 2026 that it will broaden its eligibility criteria for financing UK-based SAF projects. This expansion aims to consider a wider range of financing options, thereby opening the door to greater investment in the sector and helping projects move from development into commercial production.

Government incentives and private sector investment

The government is bolstering the SAF industry through various funding initiatives. These efforts aim to position the UK as a global hub for low-carbon fuels, fostering economic growth and job creation.

Impact on Sustainable fuel production capacity

These financing mechanisms are designed to stimulate domestic SAF production and infrastructure development. The government's vision includes having at least five commercial-scale SAF plants under construction in the UK by 2025. Increased investment is crucial to overcome the high production costs of SAF, which remain significantly more expensive than conventional jet fuels. By providing financial certainty, these initiatives aim to encourage the construction of new production plants and foster a competitive market.

Sustainable aviation fuel production pathways

SAF can be produced through various technological pathways, each utilising different feedstocks and conversion processes. The UK is exploring a range of these technologies to diversify its production capabilities.

Key technologies: HEFA, Fischer-Tropsch, and Alcohol-to-Jet

Several key pathways are approved for producing SAF. Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) is currently the most established method, converting waste oils, animal fats, and vegetable oils into jet fuel. Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis converts biomass or municipal solid waste into syngas, which is then processed into SAF. Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) technology converts alcohols like ethanol or isobutanol into jet fuel.

text:
GENEVA — The International Air Transport Association (IATA) Board of Directors has appointed World Economic Forum executive Saadia Zahidi as its next director general, choosing a leader from outside airline management as the industry confronts financial, operational, environmental, and geopolitical pressure.

Zahidi will become IATA's ninth director general and the first woman appointed to the position when she takes office on November 1, 2026. Willie Walsh will conclude his duties on July 31 after leading IATA since April 2021. Chief Financial Officer and Senior Vice President for Corporate Services Sandrine Le Borgne will serve as interim director general during the intervening three months.

Who Is Saadia Zahidi?

Zahidi is a managing director and member of the World Economic Forum's Managing Board. She founded and leads its Centre for the New Economy and Society, which works on economic growth, employment, skills, technology, and global risks.

Her World Economic Forum profile says she has also led the organization's global communications and programming groups and its engagement with civil society, academics, and international organizations. She founded and co-authors recurring research including the Future of Jobs, Future of Growth, Global Gender Gap, and Chief Economists Outlook reports.

IATA Board Chair and LATAM Airlines Group CEO Roberto Alvo said the Board selected Zahidi because technology and geopolitics will reshape aviation and because her experience can strengthen IATA's voice with governments and other stakeholders. That is the Board's stated rationale; IATA has not yet published a detailed program showing how she will apply that background to individual aviation policies.

The selection is unusual in IATA's modern history but not unprecedented. IATA's record of its directors general shows a succession of airline executives from Günter Eser's appointment in 1985 through Walsh. Earlier leaders included Knut Hammarskjöld, who came from the European Free Trade Association, and Sir William Hildred, who came from Britain's civil aviation administration.

What the IATA Director General Does

The director general is IATA's senior executive and most visible industry advocate. The role does not regulate airlines or control member-carrier operations. Instead, the director general runs the association and represents collective airline positions on safety, security, taxation, infrastructure, passenger regulation, distribution, sustainability, and other cross-border issues.

Under IATA's airline-led governance structure, its Board of Directors sets strategy, oversees finances and risk, approves key policies, and appoints the director general. Member airlines confirm the appointment at an Annual General Meeting when required. IATA has not announced whether or when that confirmation will occur for Zahidi.

IATA's role also extends well beyond advocacy. Its traffic conferences develop common standards used to sell tickets, handle cargo, and coordinate operations across borders. Membership requires registration under the IATA Operational Safety Audit, while the association operates data, training, accreditation, and financial services. Its Simplified Invoicing and Settlement platform alone settles about $83 billion in invoices annually.

Zahidi will therefore inherit both a policy mandate and an operating institution whose standards and services connect airlines with travel agents, freight forwarders, airports, suppliers, and regulators.

Why It Matters

IATA represents more than 370 airlines carrying about 85% of global air traffic. Its director general can place common airline priorities before national governments, the International Civil Aviation Organization, infrastructure providers, manufacturers, and energy producers. That influence matters most where one carrier cannot solve a problem alone.

Aircraft shortages, fragmented regulation, airspace closures, insufficient airport capacity, and limited sustainable aviation fuel supply all cross company and national boundaries. IATA cannot compel a manufacturer to deliver an aircraft or a government to change a rule, but it can define industry standards, assemble data, coordinate its membership, and press for common policy.

For travelers, the consequences are indirect but tangible. Decisions influenced by those debates can affect seat capacity, fares, disruption handling, safety processes, airport congestion, and the cost and pace of decarbonization. Airways has separately examined IATA's latest global airline safety findings and the industry's struggle to expand sustainable aviation fuel supply.

Why the Transition Is Happening Now

The confirmed public explanation is limited. Walsh will leave on July 31, and Zahidi will start on November 1. IATA's announcement does not explain why Walsh is departing, identify his next role, or say why the transition requires a three-month interim director general. A more specific causal account would be unsupported.

The handover nevertheless follows IATA's June Annual General Meeting, where Walsh identified regulation aligned with global standards, infrastructure, and decarbonization policy as the association's central advocacy priorities. It also comes as IATA replaces its former advisory councils with nine industry committees covering areas including operations, finance, cargo, security, sustainability, and digital transformation. Those are the conditions Zahidi will inherit, although IATA has not said they prompted the leadership change.

Walsh began his tenure while airlines were navigating the COVID-19 crisis and subsequently led IATA through the industry's traffic recovery and its 2021 commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. Zahidi will take over with passenger demand high but the industry's financial cushion and productive capacity under pressure.

The Issues Zahidi Will Inherit

Profitability and Geopolitics

IATA's June outlook cut its expected 2026 airline net profit to $23 billion and its net margin to 2.0%, roughly half its previous forecasts of $41 billion and 3.9%. The association expects airlines to earn $4.50 per passenger despite total industry revenue of $1.165 trillion and a record 84% passenger load factor.

IATA attributed the deterioration principally to Middle East disruption and higher fuel prices. Conflict can close airspace, lengthen routes, disrupt hubs, and complicate airport-slot rules, while trade tensions affect cargo demand and aerospace supply chains. Zahidi's experience with global economic risks aligns with that policy environment, but her effectiveness will be measurable only through the positions and agreements developed after she arrives.

Aircraft, Engines, and Infrastructure

In his June state-of-the-industry address, Walsh said the aircraft backlog exceeded 18,000, the average fleet age had reached 15.2 years, and supply-chain failures cost airlines at least $11 billion in 2025.

Delayed aircraft and engines constrain growth, increase leasing and maintenance costs, and postpone expected fuel-efficiency gains. Airlines have responded by retaining older aircraft, increasing utilization, and operating at higher load factors. IATA will continue pressing manufacturers and maintenance providers over delivery reliability, engine durability, repair capacity, and aftermarket competition.

Infrastructure is the parallel constraint. IATA says nearly 400 airports require slot coordination because demand exceeds available capacity at least some of the time. The association also argues that fragmented or aging air traffic management systems add delays, fuel burn, and cost. Zahidi will need to represent airline demands for additional capacity and modernization while contesting airport and navigation charges that carriers consider excessive.

Sustainability and Regulation

IATA says sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could deliver as much as 65% of the emissions reduction needed for net zero in 2050. Yet 2026 production is expected to reach only 2.4 million tonnes, equivalent to 0.8% of airline fuel consumption.

Closing that gap requires fuel producers to build capacity, governments to establish workable incentives and accounting rules, airports to support distribution, and manufacturers to advance aircraft technology. Airlines cannot deliver those elements alone, making cross-sector coordination central to IATA's role.

Zahidi will also inherit disputes over passenger rights, taxation, airport regulation, climate measures, cybersecurity, and data policy. IATA favors globally harmonized rules for global networks, while governments retain national authority and travelers expect effective consumer protection. The practical test will be whether the association can demonstrate where common standards improve outcomes and propose workable compliance where rules differ.

What Happens Next

Le Borgne will assume interim responsibility after Walsh leaves and remain in the role until Zahidi starts on November 1. IATA's governance rules may also require member airlines to confirm the appointment at an Annual General Meeting, but the association has not announced the timing.

Stakeholders should watch Zahidi's senior appointments, her first policy program, and the priorities advanced through IATA's new committee structure. Airlines will look for continuity on costs, infrastructure, standards, and supplier accountability. Airports and manufacturers will watch how she approaches investment and operational constraints. Regulators will look for concrete proposals rather than general calls for cooperation.

The unanswered questions remain important: why Walsh is leaving, why IATA selected a three-month interim period, when member confirmation may occur, and whether Zahidi will alter the association's positions on climate policy, passenger regulation, or supplier relations. Until IATA or Zahidi provides those answers, the appointment signals a change in leadership background—not yet a confirmed change in policy.
