text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection is adding 10 Airbus H125 helicopters to its Air and Marine Operations fleet for law enforcement, border security, and public safety missions across the country. Airbus announced the finalized deal on July 7, 2026, while federal award records put the delivery order at $95,507,814.

The most important takeaway is not simply that CBP is buying more helicopters. It is choosing a light, single-engine platform for surveillance and tactical support alongside much larger UH-60 Black Hawks, a fleet strategy that may improve mission efficiency but does not automatically make the operation environmentally friendly.

The $95.5 million deal

The final price is lower than the pre-award figure that circulated in late 2025. At that time, a Department of Homeland Security acquisition forecast described a contract worth more than $100 million for configuring and managing up to 10 H125s plus related equipment, but the May 2026 delivery order to Davenport Aviation was recorded at about $95.5 million.

This distinction matters. Forecasts are planning estimates, while awarded obligations show what the government actually committed, and the federal record describes a fixed-price order for 10 H125 light enforcement rotorcraft with a performance period running through May 26, 2028.

Airbus executive Bart Reijnen said the choice reflects the “trust placed in the H125” for demanding public-safety missions.

The new purchase follows Airbus’s 2020 order for 16 H125s, which were equipped for patrol, surveillance, and rescue work. That earlier package included infrared detection, thermal imaging, night vision compatibility, hoist capability, and loudspeakers, though Airbus has not detailed the full mission equipment fit for the 2026 batch.

Why the H125 keeps winning

The H125, previously known as the AS350 and called the AStar in North America, is built around a simple idea. Give agencies a compact aircraft that can remain on station, operate in heat and high terrain, and carry sensors without requiring a medium-lift helicopter for every call.

Airbus lists a maximum takeoff weight of 5,225 pounds, a range of 340 nautical miles, and maximum endurance of 4 hours and 27 minutes. Its Safran Arriel 2D engine produces 952 shaft horsepower, while dual-channel digital engine control, an engine data recorder, and dual hydraulic flight controls are designed to reduce pilot workload.

For CBP, the practical value is the view from the cabin and the ability to work close to ground teams. Existing H125 operations commonly use a pilot and a sensor operator, with electro-optical and infrared cameras, mapping tools, and video links helping crews follow people, vehicles, or vessels from the air.

A lighter partner to the Black Hawk

CBP also flies Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk variants for missions that need more lifting power, crew capacity, or rescue equipment. For scale, Lockheed Martin lists the UH-60M at a maximum gross weight of 22,000 pounds, more than four times the H125’s listed maximum takeoff weight.

That does not make one aircraft better than the other. A Black Hawk can handle heavy rescue, transport, and disaster response, while the H125 is better suited to many short-range observation and light enforcement tasks. In practical terms, matching the smaller helicopter to the smaller mission can avoid using a much heavier machine when it is not needed.

Using a smaller single-engine helicopter for a light surveillance task could also lower operating costs and fuel demand compared with sending a heavier twin-engine aircraft.

Still, that is a reasonable inference from aircraft size and role, not a measured environmental result from this contract, because Airbus did not publish expected annual flight hours, fuel consumption, emissions, or a comparison with the aircraft the new H125s will replace.

The environmental test

Helicopters bring environmental tradeoffs wherever they fly. Turbine fuel creates greenhouse gas emissions, while repeated low-level operations can add noise to desert, coastal, wetland, mountain, and residential areas that may already be sensitive to disturbance.

The National Park Service notes that intermittent noise and visual disturbance can be perceived by wildlife as threats and can trigger avoidance behavior. That makes route planning, altitude, time on station, and seasonal restrictions important, especially around nesting areas, migration corridors, and quiet communities.

The H125 does have a possible lower-carbon pathway. Airbus says its helicopters are certified for blends containing up to 50 percent sustainable aviation fuel, and an H125 completed a demonstration flight in China using a 40 percent blend in 2023.

But the CBP announcement contains no commitment to buy SAF, so technical compatibility should not be confused with actual emissions cuts.

Built in Mississippi

Airbus will manufacture the helicopters at its facility in Columbus, Mississippi, giving the order a clear U.S. industrial component despite the company’s European roots. The prime delivery order went to Davenport Aviation, a government aviation supplier that previously worked with Airbus and CBP on H125 procurement.

Federal award data says two bids were received and the order was placed through the Multiple Award Schedule. The procurement’s “light enforcement platform” description also indicates that the government is buying operational aircraft rather than 10 standard passenger helicopters sitting on a ramp.

What to watch next

The unanswered questions now matter more than the sales announcement. Airbus’s release did not state where the aircraft will be based, how quickly each one will enter service, which older helicopters will leave the fleet, or how many flight hours the new batch is expected to add.

Those details will determine the real operational and environmental outcome. A newer, lighter helicopter can be a smarter tool if it replaces aging aircraft, reduces maintenance downtime, and keeps Black Hawks off routine surveillance missions, but the benefit shrinks if it simply produces more total flying.

For now, the H125 order looks like a practical fleet-standardization decision with strong surveillance capability and a domestic manufacturing link.

text:
JAKARTA - PT PLN Energi Primer Indonesia (PLN EPI) memperkuat pengembangan ekosistem hidrogen rendah karbon nasional melalui rangkaian kolaborasi bisnis, pengembangan rantai pasok, dan pertukaran pengetahuan.

Dalam forum Global Hydrogen Ecosystem Summit & Exhibition (GHES) 2026 pada 21-23 Juli 2026 di Jakarta International Convention Center (JICC), PLN EPI mendorong optimalisasi potensi biomassa Indonesia sebagai bahan baku biohidrogen dan bahan bakar penerbangan berkelanjutan atau Sustainable Aviation Fuel (eSAF).

Partisipasi PLN EPI meliputi penandatanganan Nota Kesepahaman (Memorandum of Understanding/MoU) dengan perusahaan asal Singapura, eFuels SEA Pte. Ltd., serta penyampaian strategi pengembangan biohidrogen oleh jajaran perusahaan dalam dua sesi konferensi.

Langkah ini menjadi bagian dari upaya membangun rantai nilai energi rendah karbon dari sumber bahan baku, teknologi produksi, logistik, hingga pemanfaatannya oleh sektor ketenagalistrikan, transportasi, dan industri.

GHES 2026 dibuka oleh Menteri Energi dan Sumber Daya Mineral (ESDM) Bahlil Lahadalia. Dalam arahannya, Bahlil menempatkan hidrogen sebagai salah satu sumber energi masa depan yang berpotensi memperkuat kemandirian energi nasional.

"Selain itu, juga mendorong hilirisasi industri, dan melengkapi pengembangan kendaraan listrik berbasis baterai," kata Bahlil.

Pemerintah juga mendorong GHES 2026 bergerak dari tahap penyusunan peta jalan dan kesepakatan awal menuju tindak lanjut serta implementasi proyek yang lebih konkret,

Sementara itu, Sekretaris Perusahaan PLN EPI Mamit Setiawan mengatakan, keikutsertaan perusahaan dalam GHES 2026 menunjukkan komitmen PLN EPI untuk tidak hanya menjaga keandalan pasokan energi primer saat ini, tetapi juga mempersiapkan sumber energi masa depan yang lebih bersih dan berkelanjutan.

PLN EPI juga mengembangkan portofolio energi primer rendah karbon dengan mengoptimalkan kekayaan sumber daya domestik, termasuk biomassa.

"GHES 2026 menjadi momentum untuk mempertemukan potensi bahan baku Indonesia dengan teknologi, investasi, dan pasar sehingga pengembangan biohidrogen serta eSAF dapat bergerak menuju implementasi yang nyata,” ujar Mamit.

Pada hari pertama penyelenggaraan, PLN EPI dan eFuels SEA Pte. Ltd. menandatangani MoU untuk menjajaki pengembangan rantai pasok hidrogen hijau lintas batas antara Indonesia dan Singapura.

Kerja sama tersebut juga mencakup eksplorasi peluang pengembangan ekosistem eFuels, mulai dari kajian potensi bahan baku, teknologi produksi, model bisnis, hingga peluang pemanfaatan dan pemasaran produk energi rendah karbon.

Mamit menambahkan, kerja sama internasional dibutuhkan untuk mempercepat penguasaan teknologi, memperkuat kelayakan komersial, dan membuka akses terhadap pembiayaan serta pasar energi bersih.

“Pengembangan hidrogen membutuhkan ekosistem yang terintegrasi dan tidak dapat dilakukan oleh satu pihak. Melalui kolaborasi ini, PLN EPI ingin membangun fondasi rantai pasok yang kuat, kompetitif, dan berkelanjutan dengan tetap mengutamakan pemanfaatan potensi energi domestik serta penciptaan nilai tambah bagi Indonesia,” kata Mamit.

Direktur Biomassa PLN EPI Hokkop Situngkir membahas pengembangan rantai pasok, infrastruktur, dan distribusi hidrogen serta amonia rendah karbon. Dalam sesi tersebut, Hokkop memaparkan peluang mengubah keunggulan biomassa Indonesia menjadi fondasi industri hidrogen rendah karbon.

"Potensi tersebut tidak hanya dapat dimanfaatkan untuk program co-firing pada pembangkit listrik tenaga uap, tetapi juga dikembangkan menjadi biohidrogen, biogas, biochar, eSAF, dan berbagai produk energi bernilai tambah lainnya," ujarnya.

Menurut Mamit, biomassa memberikan peluang strategis bagi Indonesia karena mampu menghubungkan agenda transisi energi dengan pengelolaan limbah, pemberdayaan masyarakat, pengembangan ekonomi sirkular, dan pertumbuhan industri hijau.

“Indonesia memiliki sumber biomassa yang besar dan tersebar di berbagai daerah. Dengan dukungan teknologi serta rantai pasok yang tepat, potensi tersebut dapat ditingkatkan menjadi produk energi rendah karbon yang memberikan manfaat bagi sistem kelistrikan, industri, transportasi, masyarakat, dan perekonomian nasional,” jelas Mamit.

GHES 2026 menjadi forum yang mempertemukan pemerintah, pelaku industri, akademisi, lembaga riset, investor, penyedia teknologi, dan mitra global dalam mempercepat pembentukan ekosistem hidrogen nasional.

Pemerintah memandang hidrogen berperan penting dalam mendukung dekarbonisasi sektor industri berat dan transportasi jarak jauh yang relatif sulit dialihkan sepenuhnya melalui elektrifikasi.

Delta Signs Five-Year Agreement with Shell Aviation for SAF Use

Delta Air Lines has signed a five-year agreement with Shell Aviation, valid through 2030, to increase the supply of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Under the collaboration, SAF supply is planned at key hubs and priority locations across the U.S., including Los Angeles, Portland, New York JFK, Boston Logan and Minneapolis-St. Paul airports.

The agreement covers not only fuel supply but also the development of the infrastructure required for the transportation, blending, storage and distribution of SAF. Shell Aviation will support the delivery of both blended and neat SAF at selected hubs, contributing to a more reliable and consistent supply system for Delta’s operations.

The collaboration between Delta and Shell aims to make SAF a regular part of the airline’s daily operations rather than a one-off initiative. The agreement is expected to strengthen Delta’s fuel diversification as well as its access to sustainable aviation fuel and long-term supply capacity.

text:
Jet Aviation’s new FBO at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport is now fully operational.

The 27-acre facility includes an 8,500-square-foot terminal.

There is 40,000 square feet of new hangarage.

The unit of General Dynamics launched initial operations at the site in November 2025 with a temporary terminal building.

The permanent facility is an 8,500-square-foot FBO building with a 540,000-square-foot ramp capable of accommodating larger-cabin, ultra-long-range business jets.

There are two taxiway connections into the airport system, fueling with Jet-A, 100LL, and sustainable aviation fuel, and drive-on access to the ramp via a private entrance.

On-site Customs and Border Protection is scheduled to open in Q3 2026.

President Jeremie Caillet said, “Our entry into Miami-Opa Locka marks a significant milestone for Jet Aviation.”

He added, “As one of the busiest business aviation gateways in the Americas, Miami is a key destination for customers around the world, connecting them to North America, Latin America, the Caribbean, and beyond.”

The modern architecture and interior design draw on a classic Miami aesthetic, with an open-plan layout and floor-to-ceiling windows providing unobstructed airside views to the ramp and runway.

Amenities included dedicated office spaces, guest and crew lounge areas, and a private conference room.

The facility is built to LEED standards and features solar panels, low-flow water fixtures, and LED lighting.

There is also AV and EV charging.

Miami is the company’s 12th FBO in the U.S.

It is the 7th busiest private jet airport in the country.

The Gulfstream Aerospace sister company has 30 worldwide.

“I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative,” said Julie Kitcher, Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications, Airbus.

text:
Air Canada and Airbus are uniting their shared commitment to aviation decarbonisation, announcing their intent to establish a jointly funded Sustainability Co-Investment Platform. This agreement states a shared objective to invest up to approximately C$13.7 million (US$10 million), through the platform to support a commercial-scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry in Canada. Both companies are confident that, with a supportive public policy framework in place, this investment can serve as a catalyst for the broader Canadian SAF ecosystem.

“Air Canada is proud to help advance aviation’s energy transition in Canada,” said Valerie Durand, Vice President, Airport Affairs, Corporate Real Estate and Sustainability, Air Canada. “Through this joint initiative with Airbus, we are taking meaningful steps toward supporting domestic SAF production, helping corporate customers address the emissions associated with business travel, and contributing to a lower-carbon path for the industry. With continued industry collaboration and a supportive policy environment, we are confident this momentum can accelerate.”

Key focus areas include accelerating a jointly agreed Canadian SAF project toward a Final Investment Decision (FID). While Air Canada and Airbus intend to drive this investment, both companies look forward to continuing their constructive collaboration with government partners to establish the right structural frameworks to support SAF production to emerge at scale in Canada. Their ongoing joint advocacy alongside the Canadian Council for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (C-SAF) reflects a shared commitment to working with federal and provincial governments. By aligning industry initiatives with supportive public policy mechanisms, they can successfully champion domestic SAF production and price competitiveness, with the objective to make renewable fuels available for the Canadian aerospace industry and to preserve affordability of air travel.

“I want to thank Air Canada for this very important joint sustainability initiative,” said Julie Kitcher, Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications, Airbus. “Decarbonising aviation will require deep industry collaboration and decades of investment in new sources of renewable energy. By launching this co-investment platform and making a long-term commitment to Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Programme, we will help to stimulate the production of, and demand for, SAF in Canada. The country has a vast feedstock potential. When combined with a supportive policy framework, it can contribute to the sector’s decarbonisation ambitions and create significant economic growth and job creation.”

Complementing this foundational investment, the initiative introduces a vehicle for corporate partners to stimulate domestic SAF demand through Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel Program. Demonstrating its commitment, Airbus has signed a long-term, five-year Leave Less Travel Program Agreement. As part of this parallel corporate travel partnership, which distributes verified SAF environmental attributes to participants, Airbus will purchase SAF environmental attributes associated with over 60,000 litres of SAF for its first allocation. Through this programme, Air Canada will track Airbus’ greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with its corporate travel and remove verified SAF environmental attributes on the company’s behalf. Although in-sector emissions reductions are not a substitute for direct emissions reductions at the source, this corporate partnership is a key tool in supporting the scaling up of SAF and will allow Airbus to lower lifecycle emissions associated with its employees’ business travel.

Hear more from Air Canada at the 20th anniversary FTE Global, taking place in Dallas, Texas, on 8 to 10 September 2026. Tom Stevens, VP Customer Experience and Service Operations, Air Canada, is participating in a session titled ‘Towards the smart apron: Automating the turnaround process’.

The fuel shipment was linked to concerns around supply stability in the United States aviation market, particularly in regions where airports depend heavily on limited fuel pipelines, storage facilities and local distribution networks.

For travellers, this development shows why fuel availability has become a major factor affecting flight schedules, ticket prices and tourism confidence. Airlines and airports worldwide are now investing in stronger fuel supply systems to prevent delays during emergencies, extreme weather events, geopolitical tensions and unexpected disruptions.

Why US Airlines Are Strengthening Jet Fuel Supply Security As Travel Demand Continues Rising

The aviation industry depends on a complex fuel network that connects refineries, pipelines, storage terminals, airports and aircraft. Any disruption at one stage can create operational challenges for airlines.

The United States has one of the largest aviation markets in the world. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), jet fuel consumption in the country remains a major component of petroleum demand, with millions of barrels used every month to support commercial aviation operations.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also highlights that airport infrastructure, including fuel systems, plays a critical role in maintaining safe and reliable air transportation.

Southwest’s decision reflects a wider industry trend where airlines are creating backup fuel solutions instead of depending on a single supply route.

The strategy helps airlines reduce risks linked to:

pipeline interruptions

refinery problems

hurricanes and extreme weather

geopolitical disruptions

sudden increases in travel demand

For passengers, stronger fuel planning means fewer unexpected cancellations and more reliable holiday and business travel.

Southwest Fuel Shipment Shows A Growing Global Airline Fuel Resilience Strategy

Southwest Airlines is not alone in preparing stronger fuel protection systems. Airlines and airports in several countries have adopted similar approaches, including maintaining larger fuel reserves, securing alternative transportation methods and diversifying fuel suppliers.

United States – Airlines Protecting Domestic Connectivity

In the US, airlines operating from major hubs have increasingly focused on fuel resilience because airports can experience supply pressure during storms, infrastructure failures and energy market volatility.

Airports such as those serving major tourism gateways in Florida, Texas, California and Hawaii are particularly sensitive because passenger demand can rise sharply during holidays and peak travel seasons.

Southwest’s fuel movement strategy demonstrates how airlines are looking beyond traditional pipelines and using alternative logistics networks to maintain operations.

Australia – Airlines Preparing For Remote Aviation Challenges

Australia’s aviation market faces unique fuel challenges because of its vast geography. Remote airports often require careful fuel planning because alternative supply options can be limited.

Airlines operating long domestic routes must maintain reliable fuel access to protect connections between major cities and regional tourism destinations.

Europe – Airlines Focus On Energy Security

European carriers have also increased attention on aviation fuel security following energy market uncertainty and geopolitical pressures.

Airlines across Europe have invested in fuel diversification, sustainable aviation fuel programmes and stronger supply agreements to reduce vulnerability.

Middle East – Aviation Hubs Build Strategic Fuel Protection

Major aviation hubs in the Middle East, including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, rely heavily on aviation as a driver of tourism and international connectivity.

Airports in the region maintain advanced fuel infrastructure because millions of passengers connect through these global travel gateways every year.

United States Tourism Corridors

Popular destinations including:

Florida

Hawaii

California

Texas

Nevada

could face higher travel pressure because these regions depend heavily on air connectivity.

A disruption in fuel availability can create:

flight reductions

longer delays

higher operating costs

increased ticket prices

Tourism businesses including hotels, cruise operators and local attractions can also experience indirect effects if visitors delay or cancel trips.

Island Destinations Face Greater Risks

Island destinations are among the most vulnerable because air travel is often the primary connection for international visitors.

Countries and regions dependent on tourism must maintain strong aviation fuel supply systems to protect visitor arrivals.

Aviation fuel security has therefore become a tourism protection issue, not just an airline operational issue.

Government Statistics Show Why Aviation Fuel Security Matters For Global Travel

The importance of reliable aviation fuel supplies is supported by government data.

According to the US Energy Information Administration, transportation remains the largest petroleum-consuming sector in the United States, showing how heavily mobility systems depend on fuel availability.

The Federal Aviation Administration reports that the US aviation system supports millions of passenger journeys annually, making reliable airport infrastructure essential for economic activity and tourism growth.

These figures demonstrate why airlines are investing in fuel resilience strategies. A stable aviation network supports jobs, tourism businesses and international connectivity.

How Travellers Can Protect Their Trips During Aviation Fuel Disruptions

Passengers cannot control fuel markets, but they can reduce travel risks by planning carefully.

Book Flexible Tickets

Travellers should consider airlines offering flexible booking options, especially during periods of global uncertainty.

Check Airline Updates Before Departure

Fuel-related disruptions can change quickly. Passengers should check:

airline mobile apps

airport websites

official travel alerts

before leaving for the airport.

Avoid Tight Connections

During operational disruptions, flights may experience delays. Longer connection times can reduce missed-flight risks.

Travel During Less Busy Periods

Peak holiday periods create additional pressure on aviation systems. Travelling during quieter periods may provide more flexibility.

Airlines Turn Fuel Security Into A New Era Of Reliable Travel

The movement of 12.6 million gallons of jet fuel by boat represents a larger transformation happening across global aviation.

Airlines are recognising that reliable flights require more than modern aircraft. They require strong fuel networks, advanced infrastructure and emergency planning.

For travellers, these investments can create a more stable travel experience with fewer disruptions and stronger confidence when booking flights.

As global tourism continues expanding, aviation fuel resilience will become one of the most important factors shaping the future of international connectivity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Southwest Airlines used marine transportation as part of a fuel supply strategy designed to improve reliability and protect operations from possible supply disruptions.

Yes. If airports or airlines cannot access sufficient fuel supplies, operations may face delays, schedule reductions or cancellations.

3. Which airports are most vulnerable to aviation fuel problems?

Airports in island destinations, remote regions and areas dependent on limited fuel pipelines may face higher risks during supply disruptions.

Fuel costs are one of the largest airline expenses. Higher fuel costs can influence airline pricing decisions.

Passengers should monitor airline notifications, airport updates and official travel information before departure.

title: Heart Aerospace X1 Clears FAA for First Flight as World's Largest Electric Aircraft
description:
How Independent Hybrid Propulsion Actually Works Heart's shift to the Independent Hybrid design in 2024 reversed an earlier architecture.
What Airlines Have Already Committed Heart Aerospace is not simply a demonstration program — it carries substantial confirmed commercial orders.
Air Canada holds a firm purchase order for 30 aircraft and has made a direct investment in Heart Aerospace.
Can Heart Reach 2031 — and What the Pattern Says The aviation industry's experience with electric aircraft startups is instructive.
Frequently Asked Questions What exactly does the FAA's Special Airworthiness Certificate allow Heart Aerospace to do?
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a Special Airworthiness Certificate in the Experimental Category (SAC-EC) to Heart Aerospace on July 23, 2026, authorizing the company to immediately begin piloted flight testing of its X1 demonstrator aircraft at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York. At 106 feet (32 meters) in wingspan, 76 feet (23 meters) in length, and more than 25,000 pounds (11,340 kg) at takeoff weight, the X1 is now the largest electric aircraft ever to receive FAA authorization for piloted flight.

The certificate marks the end of a ground-based validation campaign that stretched more than a year. The X1 completed structural, propulsion, and systems testing, along with low- and high-speed taxi trials before the FAA conducted an on-site inspection of the aircraft at Plattsburgh. In late May 2026, the X1 finished its low-speed taxi phase at the company's Plattsburgh flight-test base — the final major ground milestone before FAA review.

Anders Forslund, founder and CEO of Heart Aerospace, said the regulatory authorization represents the program's most important milestone to date: "Earning FAA flight authorization brings the X1 program to the threshold of first flight. This achievement reflects the rigor of the work completed by Heart's engineering and flight-test teams, as well as the close working relationship we have built with the FAA. With our certificate now in hand, our full focus is on flight. We are ready to get X1 in the air."

No specific date has been announced for the first flight, though the company confirmed the X1 is immediately cleared to proceed.

FAA Inspected the Aircraft, Reviewed Documentation, Then Said Yes

The certificate did not arrive automatically. The FAA conducted a full inspection of the X1 at its Plattsburgh base, reviewed the aircraft's technical documentation, and evaluated Heart's proposed flight-test operations before issuing the certificate. The review capped more than a year of coordination between Heart's engineering teams and the agency.

Cole Randle, Heart's Head of Corporate Affairs, pointed to the FAA's posture as meaningful in itself: "The agency's forward-looking approach to next-generation aircraft is accelerating commercial aviation's entry into the electric era of flight while supporting Heart's mission to lower the cost of air travel." The FAA has also provided Heart Aerospace with a $4.1 million grant under its Fuelling Aviation's Sustainable Transition (FAST) program to support development of the ES-30's hybrid-electric propulsion system.

The program has experienced delays. Heart originally targeted the X1's first flight for 2025, postponing it first to early 2026 and eventually to the current open-ended readiness status. The aircraft also required a wing component replacement following composite materials issues before it could be transferred from Sweden to Plattsburgh.

What the X1 Is, and What It Is Not

Understanding what the SAC-EC authorizes — and what it does not — is central to reading this milestone correctly.

The X1 is an all-electric demonstrator. It is powered by four 400-kilowatt electric motors manufactured by the Italian firm Phase. It carries no turboprop engines. Its flight-test campaign will generate data on aerodynamic behavior, handling characteristics, and electric systems performance for a 106-foot-wingspan aircraft of the X1's weight class. It will not generate data on the propulsion architecture that the commercial ES-30 will actually use.

The ES-30, Heart's planned 30-seat regional airliner, uses an entirely different propulsion arrangement. Under what Heart calls its Independent Hybrid system, the ES-30 will carry two large inboard electric motors — each producing 1,600 kilowatts of power — and two outboard turboprop engines operating from off-the-shelf hardware. The "independent" in the name is technically precise: each subsystem can operate the aircraft without the other. The electric side alone can fly the plane up to 125 miles (200 km) with 30 passengers and zero emissions; the turboprops extend that range to 500 miles (800 km) with 25 passengers.

The gap between what the X1 tests and what the ES-30 needs is bridged by the X2 — Heart's second full-scale demonstrator, which is scheduled to fly with the hybrid propulsion system in 2026. That flight will be the first time the Independent Hybrid system operates in the air.

How Independent Hybrid Propulsion Actually Works

Heart's shift to the Independent Hybrid design in 2024 reversed an earlier architecture. The original ES-30 concept used a serial hybrid arrangement: battery-powered electric motors for primary propulsion, supplemented by turbogenerators in the rear fuselage that burned sustainable aviation fuel to recharge the batteries and extend range. The problem was economic — turbogenerators would have been used on only a small fraction of the ES-30's flights, making them expensive to develop, certify, and maintain for rare use cases.

The current design replaces the turbogenerators with actual turboprop engines mounted outboard on the wing — the same kind of engine used on conventional turboprop airliners, available off-the-shelf and already certified. This means the electric and combustion systems can each serve as the aircraft's primary propulsion independently, rather than one system always serving the other. When both run together, the combined thrust enables a takeoff performance advantage as well.

The battery pack targeting the ES-30 is designed for approximately 330 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg) at the pack level. For context, conventional lithium-ion cells in 2018 achieved roughly 160 Wh/kg at the pack level; aviation fuel provides the energy equivalent of around 12,500 Wh/kg. Heart's target of 330 Wh/kg would represent a significant step toward commercial viability for short-haul electric flight, but still keeps the ES-30's all-electric range tightly bounded at 125 miles — which is precisely why the turboprops are there for longer routes.

The battery partnership for the ES-30 pack is with BAE Systems, which brings aerospace-grade safety-critical systems expertise and more than 25 years of electrifying large industrial vehicles. The pack was relocated from the underside of the fuselage to the rear fuselage in the redesign — a change that improved both crashworthiness and drag characteristics.

From Sweden to Upstate New York

Heart Aerospace was founded in 2018 by Anders and Klara Forslund in Gothenburg, Sweden, as a government-supported aerospace research initiative that evolved through Y Combinator's 2019 batch into a funded startup. The company first pursued the ES-19, a 19-seat all-electric aircraft targeting a 2026 service entry — a timeline that was ultimately abandoned as battery energy density proved insufficient for commercial operations at that scale. In 2022, Heart unveiled the ES-30, the hybrid-electric successor that trades raw electric ambition for practical economics.

In April 2025, the company closed its Swedish operations entirely and relocated its headquarters to Los Angeles, citing proximity to its largest investors, customers, and the broader US aerospace supply chain. The X1 had already been transferred to Plattsburgh following the wing repair work.

Heart selected Plattsburgh International Airport for its low air traffic density, airfield infrastructure, and what the company describes as strong regional support for next-generation transportation initiatives. Plattsburgh sits in the Champlain Valley near the New York-Vermont border — a geography whose wide open skies and limited commercial traffic make it well-suited to experimental flight operations.

What Airlines Have Already Committed

Heart Aerospace is not simply a demonstration program — it carries substantial confirmed commercial orders. The company's order book stands at $9.4 billion as of July 2026.

United Airlines and its regional partner Mesa Air Group — which has since merged into Republic Airways Holdings — each hold orders for 100 ES-30 aircraft. Air Canada holds a firm purchase order for 30 aircraft and has made a direct investment in Heart Aerospace. JSX has also signed a letter of intent covering up to 100 ES-30 aircraft.

The financial backing from major carriers reflects a specific market calculation: sub-500-mile routes account for the dominant share of US domestic aviation activity, and those routes are precisely where Heart claims the ES-30 is most economically competitive. At a 2031 entry into service, Heart projects the ES-30's direct operating costs at roughly 52% of those of a 50-seat regional jet — a cost reduction that would make currently unviable thin routes economical again.

Can Heart Reach 2031 — and What the Pattern Says

The aviation industry's experience with electric aircraft startups is instructive. Leeham News, which provides detailed analytical coverage of commercial aircraft programs, observed in 2024 that Heart Aerospace has "followed the typical trajectory for an electric aircraft startup" — beginning with an all-electric, battery-based concept and progressively discovering that real-world constraints force a transition through serial hybrid and ultimately parallel hybrid architectures. The observation is not a criticism so much as a pattern — Zunum Aero followed it and failed; Heart has adapted rather than collapsed.

The ES-30's certification target has itself slipped: the ES-19 targeted 2026, the original ES-30 targeted 2028, the revised target became 2029, and the most current figure from Heart's official website is a 2031 entry into service. Each slip has been accompanied by a substantive program change that arguably improved the design's commercial viability. Whether 2031 holds will depend significantly on how quickly the X1 flight-test campaign yields usable data, how rapidly the X2's hybrid-system flights proceed, and whether regulators develop clear frameworks for Part 25 certification of a novel propulsion architecture.

The FAA's $4.1 million FAST grant and its characterization of its own posture as "forward-looking" suggest the agency is not a passive observer in this timeline — it is actively invested in making electric regional aviation work within a regulatory framework it is helping to shape.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly does the FAA's Special Airworthiness Certificate allow Heart Aerospace to do?

The SAC-EC authorizes Heart to conduct piloted experimental flight tests of the X1 demonstrator at Plattsburgh International Airport. It does not permit commercial passenger operations — that would require a full FAA Type Certificate under Part 25, which is a separate, multi-year process. The X1 will fly with a test crew, gathering data on aerodynamic behavior, handling qualities, and electric systems performance. Passenger service on the production ES-30 remains targeted for 2031.

How does the X1's propulsion system differ from the commercial ES-30 Heart plans to sell?

The X1 is powered entirely by four 400-kilowatt electric motors made by the Italian firm Phase — no turboprops, no hybrid system. The commercial ES-30 uses an entirely different Independent Hybrid design: two large 1,600-kilowatt inboard electric motors that can fly the plane up to 125 miles (200 km) on battery power alone, plus two outboard turboprop engines that extend range to 500 miles (800 km). The X1 validates the aerodynamics and flight characteristics of the design; a second demonstrator, the X2, is scheduled to fly with the actual hybrid propulsion system and will be the first air validation of the propulsion architecture that paying passengers would eventually experience.

What airlines have ordered the ES-30, and how firm are those commitments?

United Airlines and Mesa Air Group (now merged into Republic Airways Holdings) each hold 100 orders; Air Canada holds 30 firm orders and has made a direct equity investment in Heart Aerospace. The combined order book stands at $9.4 billion as of July 2026. These are purchase commitments — though like all aircraft purchase agreements, they include cancellation provisions and are contingent on the aircraft receiving type certification.

description:

Participating in PCM is free thanks to support from partners like the Nebraska Corn Board.
Precision Conservation Management (PCM) is a program of the Illinois Corn Growers Association that connects grain farmers with free, one-on-one conservation support.

text:
LINCOLN, Neb. – Precision Conservation Management (PCM) is expanding its Nebraska presence with the addition of two new regions, bringing the program’s free, one-on-one farm data analysis to grain producers in Northeast and Southeast Nebraska for the first time.

PCM has been serving Nebraska farmers in the Gothenburg and York regions for several years in partnership with the Nebraska Corn Board and local Natural Resource Districts. The addition of the Norfolk and Beatrice regions means more Nebraska producers now have direct access to a local PCM specialist who can analyze their field data and help farmers make decisions grounded in profitability, not guesswork.

PCM was created by IL Corn in 2015 to utilize field-level data to analyze the financial outcomes of tillage, nitrogen management, and cover crop decisions, providing farmers with a clear picture of how these practices impact their bottom line. Participating in PCM is free thanks to support from partners like the Nebraska Corn Board. There are no requirements to change farming practices, and all farm data is immediately anonymized upon enrollment.

“The growth of the Precision Conservation Management Program in Nebraska means farmers have greater access to resources that help them farm better using data-driven conservation tools,” said Rachael Whitehair, director of innovation and stewardship for the Nebraska Corn Board. “At a time when farmers need to know their best and most efficient options, PCM is a tool that helps lead them to success.”

In addition to one-on-one specialist support, enrolled farmers gain access to cost-share and incentive programs through PCM as well as advice on other programs they might be eligible for. Enrollers also receive an annual Resource Analysis and Assessment Plan (RAAP) report each February, providing a field-by-field breakdown of financial and environmental outcomes of in-field practices.

Meet the New Specialists

Frank Lammers — Norfolk Region

Frank Lammers brings a background in agronomy and hands-on farm experience to his role as PCM’s Conservation Specialist for the Norfolk region. Based in Northeast Nebraska, Frank works with producers to use field-level data to evaluate conservation practices against real profitability outcomes. Living and working on a farm himself, he brings a practical perspective that resonates with producers who want answers grounded in how things actually work in the field.

Email: [email protected]

Tyler Ottensmeier — Beatrice Region

Tyler Ottensmeier brings more than 11 years of agricultural financial services experience to his role as PCM’s Conservation Specialist for the Beatrice region. His background as an agricultural loan officer gives him a firsthand understanding of how farm financial decisions get made and what it takes for a practice change to make economic sense. Tyler also operates a cow-calf and farming operation in Southeast Nebraska, keeping him closely connected to the producers he serves.

Email: [email protected]

How to Get Started

Nebraska grain farmers interested in enrolling in PCM can visit precisionconservation.org/farmers to learn more and fill out a brief interest form. A PCM Specialist will follow up to walk through the enrollment process.

Precision Conservation Management (PCM) is a program of the Illinois Corn Growers Association that connects grain farmers with free, one-on-one conservation support. PCM’s regional Conservation Specialists use field-level data to help farmers evaluate the profitability of tillage, nitrogen management, and cover crop practices — with no cost to enroll and no requirement to change farming practices. PCM currently operates in Illinois, Nebraska, Kentucky, and Missouri. Learn more at precisionconservation.org.

The Nebraska Corn Board is funded through a producer checkoff investment of a 1-cent-per-bushel on all corn marketed in the state and is managed by nine farmer directors. The mission of the Nebraska Corn Board is to increase the value and sustainability of Nebraska corn through promotion, market development and research.

— Nebraska Corn Board

title: Nebraska Corn Board Enters 2026-2027 Fiscal Year with Expanded Reach, Continued Momentum
description:
– A new fiscal year is underway at the Nebraska Corn Board, and with it comes a lineup of new and growing initiatives funded through the corn checkoff for 2026-2027.
Market Development Market development programs continue driving demand for Nebraska corn through ethanol, trade and livestock expansion and emerging market opportunities.
In partnership with the Nebraska Ethanol Board, NCB will continue demonstrations exploring E30 in non-flex-fuel vehicles.
The Nebraska Corn Board is funded through a producer checkoff investment of a 1-cent-per-bushel on all corn marketed in the state and is managed by nine farmer directors.
The mission of the Nebraska Corn Board is to increase the value and sustainability of Nebraska corn through promotion, market development and research.
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. – A new fiscal year is underway at the Nebraska Corn Board, and with it comes a lineup of new and growing initiatives funded through the corn checkoff for 2026-2027. Every dollar is directed through NCB’s strategic plan, which organizes checkoff investments around four pillars: education, promotion, market development and research, with a clear focus on the return those investments generate for Nebraska corn farmers and the state’s economy.

NCB continues to collaborate with state, national and international partners like the Alliance for the Future of Agriculture in Nebraska (AFAN), National Corn Growers Association, U.S. Grains and BioProducts Council and U.S. Meat Export Federation to drive demand and increase the value of Nebraska corn.

Education and Promotion

For 2026-2027, NCB is expanding its partnership with the Omaha Supernovas, continuing for the second year a “Farmers’ Appreciation Night” featured match, season-long court signage and a branded media backdrop activation that deepens NCB’s reach with fans across 180-plus Nebraska communities and 40 states through live events and broadcast visibility.

NCB is also continuing its partnership with Agriculture in the Classroom, partnering to extend the program’s reach into underserved communities; last year the program reached more than 19,700 students through 1,102 lessons and trained 425 educators.

NCB is also partnering with the Big Ten Network to share the message of homegrown ethanol and E15 with nearly 30 million viewers nationwide. These partnerships and others continue to broaden NCB’s reach in support of market development and research.

Market Development

Market development programs continue driving demand for Nebraska corn through ethanol, trade and livestock expansion and emerging market opportunities. Efforts include supporting ethanol infrastructure in Nebraska and key markets such as California, where demand for E85 continues to grow. Last year, these efforts helped 22 Nebraska locations add higher ethanol blends, intending to add 25 more this year. In California, NCB is working with Pearson Fuels to expand its network to 550 E85 locations across the West Coast.

In partnership with the Nebraska Ethanol Board, NCB will continue demonstrations exploring E30 in non-flex-fuel vehicles. The project has used more than 737,000 gallons of E30 to demonstrate vehicles can operate on higher ethanol blends. Additional research is evaluating fuel retail rewards programs to increase E15 purchases, following an initial study that found 41% of participants continued purchasing E15 after the promotion ended.

Beyond on-road transportation, NCB continues to evaluate ethanol opportunities in sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and maritime shipping, where feasibility work indicates the industry could create demand for more than 5-6 billion gallons of ethanol annually.

Livestock development remains a key priority, with continued support for AFAN and specific projects that expand demand for corn through beef, swine, poultry and dairy sectors. Over the past two years, 24.6 million bushels of new demand have strengthened Nebraska’s value-added opportunities.

As global trade continues to evolve, Nebraska Corn remains committed to engaging with the current trade dynamics at play. Nebraska Corn will be hosting 3 international trade delegations over the next several months to educate international customers overseas and strengthen relationships, in addition to engaging with several other international representatives as they tour Nebraska. U.S. exports of corn and ethanol are on pace to set back-to-back record years.

Research

NCB is actively driving demand and profitability for Nebraska corn and ethanol. Six new end-use projects spanning biobased polymer coatings, industrial chemicals, and human nutrition are in development with the potential to unlock more than 2.5 billion bushels of additional annual demand. On the feed side, today’s favorable distillers grain prices create a strategic opening to grow market share in cattle rations, supported by both biological and economic evidence.

For farmers battling rising input costs, two key programs are delivering real ROI. The Nebraska Nitrogen Initiative empowers farmers to conduct N-rate small plot trials, bringing data-driven precision to nitrogen decisions that can vary by as much as 100% from field to field and year to year, turning information into savings. Precision Conservation Management has expanded to two new Nebraska regions. This free agronomic service analyzes farm data to identify exactly which management decisions are profitable and which aren’t. Growers even receive $500 in year one for participating.

NCB is committed to being a strategic partner in Nebraska’s growing bioeconomy. Six new end-use projects spanning biobased polymer coatings, corn-derived industrial chemicals and precision human nutrition are in development, with the potential to unlock more than 2.5 billion bushels of additional annual demand. Corn-derived industrial chemicals are a particularly active area of research, as these compounds feed into thousands of everyday products in markets currently dominated by petroleum-derived alternatives. NCB is funding research that moves beyond proof of concept to focus on scaling and commercialization.

“This year’s investments reflect our commitment to putting Nebraska corn in front of more farmers and consumers in more targeted places than ever before,” said Andy Groskopf, chairman of NCB. “Every checkoff dollar is directed toward programs proven to deliver a return, whether that’s building new markets for our grain, strengthening consumer trust, or reaching the next generation of Nebraskans. We’re confident these partnerships in promotion, market development and research will keep Nebraska corn, and our farmers, moving forward.”

Learn more about the programs funded by the Nebraska Corn Board at nebraskacorn.gov.

The Nebraska Corn Board is funded through a producer checkoff investment of a 1-cent-per-bushel on all corn marketed in the state and is managed by nine farmer directors. The mission of the Nebraska Corn Board is to increase the value and sustainability of Nebraska corn through promotion, market development and research.
